section: The heart that turns, and the heart that does not
paragraph: And some cover the danger over with false peace. "You say, 'I am innocent; surely his anger has turned from me'" (Jeremiah 2:35). Prophets "say continually to those who despise the word of the Lord, 'It shall be well with you'" (Jeremiah 23:17). John the Baptist meets the same thing: "do not presume to say to yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father'" (Matthew 3:9).

Desire can take hold in the heart before anything is done. Jesus says, "everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart" (Matthew 5:28). The way in is the eye, and he goes straight on: "If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away" (5:29). Proverbs warns a son in the same order, heart and eyes: "Do not desire her beauty in your heart, and do not let her capture you with her eyelashes" (Proverbs 6:25). The Preacher uses the hunter's picture for the other side of that capture: "the woman whose heart is snares and nets, and whose hands are fetters. He who pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is taken by her" (Ecclesiastes 7:26). He names it as his own finding, after he had "turned my heart to know and to search out" (7:25). The escape he names is not strength of will but pleasing God.

Anxiety, as the verses show it, is a mind and heart taken up with something not yet made safe: food and clothing, tomorrow, what to say before a court, other people, one's own sin. Proverbs gives it weight: "Anxiety in a man's heart weighs him down, but a good word makes him glad" (Proverbs 12:25). Jesus names what it is usually about: "do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you will put on" (Matthew 6:25). Here "life" is the life that needs feeding, and Luke's version gives the reason not to be anxious: "For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing" (Luke 12:23).

The same feeling is not always the same thing.
- **Anger** can heal, as Jesus's does (Mark 3:5). It can stop its ears and stone a man (Acts 7:57–58). It can be "a rage that has reached up to heaven" (2 Chronicles 28:9). "Be angry and do not sin" (Ephesians 4:26) tells me anger itself is not forbidden. What it does, and how long it stays, is the question.
- **Indignation** is the disciples' complaint at a woman's gift: "Why this waste?" (Matthew 26:8). It is also one of the fruits of a grief that turns to God: "what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal" (2 Corinthians 7:11).
- **Vexation**, *ka'as*, is what a person does to another ("her rival used to provoke her grievously", 1 Samuel 1:6), what a person bears ("I have been speaking out of my great anxiety and vexation", 1:16), and even something that does good: "Sorrow is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad" (Ecclesiastes 7:3). The verse before gives the house of mourning its reason: "for this is the end of all mankind, and the living will lay it to heart" (7:2).
- **Fear** is forbidden and commanded, sometimes in one sentence (Exodus 20:20). The word for the fear that makes people run is the word for the fear that keeps them from turning away. The section on fear above sets out what changes it.
- **Anxiety** is rebuked when it is for my own food and clothing (Matthew 6:25), and praised when it is for the welfare of others (Philippians 2:20). It is the same Greek word. The Hebrew word for anxious dread is also the word for being sorry for sin (Psalm 38:18). The section on anxiety above sets out the difference.
- **Provoking** is what love does not do. It "is not irritable" (1 Corinthians 13:5). Yet believers are told, "let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works" (Hebrews 10:24), with the same Greek word.
- **Delight** is set on God's commandments by the man who fears him (Psalm 112:1), and on war by the peoples God scatters (Psalm 68:30). The same claim about God's delight is thanks in one psalm and a taunt in another (Psalm 18:19; 22:8). The section on delight above sets out what it is set on.

- **A tender heart.** It melts before an enemy and spreads fear to others (Deuteronomy 20:8). But Josiah's heart "was penitent [tender]" before God's word, and God answered him with peace (2 Kings 22:19–20). The same softness is cowardice in one place and repentance in the other.
- **A strong heart.** "Be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the Lord!" (Psalm 27:14). With Absalom, the same verb gives his servants the nerve to kill: "be courageous and be valiant" (2 Samuel 13:28). With Pharaoh it is hardening: "I will harden his heart" (Exodus 4:21), literally *strengthen*.
- **A guarded heart.** "Keep your heart with all vigilance" (Proverbs 4:23). Three chapters later the same word describes the adulteress, "wily [guarded] of heart" (Proverbs 7:10).
- **Crushing.** Crushed by an enemy, the spirit collapses (Psalm 143:3–4). Offered to God, a crushed spirit is the very sacrifice he wants: "a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (Psalm 51:17).
- **Loving and hating one's own soul** (Chapter 5).
- **Devising.** The same Hebrew verb describes the craftsmen who worked cherubim "skillfully" into the tabernacle curtains (Exodus 26:1) and those who plot. One word for planning means "discretion" (Proverbs 2:11), "evil devices" (Proverbs 12:2), and God's own purpose: "no purpose of yours can be thwarted" (Job 42:2).
- **Planning against.** God says, "I am … devising a plan against you. Return" (Jeremiah 18:11), and the people say, "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah" (18:18). The word and the "against" are the same. One plan is meant to bring people back, and the other is meant to silence the one who calls them.
- **Purposing.** The verb for purposing (*zāmam*) is the psalmist's resolve: "I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress" (Psalm 17:3). It is the wicked man's plot: "The wicked plots against the righteous" (Psalm 37:12). It is the wise woman's weighing: "She considers a field and buys it" (Proverbs 31:16). And it is God's fixed purpose: "I have purposed; I have not relented" (Jeremiah 4:28). I read the change as following whom it is aimed at: one's own mouth, another's harm, one's own household, or a whole land.
- **Willing.** The Hebrew word for being willing (*ʾāḇâ*) is almost always a "no". It is the guard's refusal to kill the priests (1 Samuel 22:17), David refusing the water for the men's sake (2 Samuel 23:17), Amnon refusing Tamar's plea (2 Samuel 13:14), and Israel refusing God's rest (Isaiah 30:15). God himself is "not willing to destroy" (2 Kings 8:19), and "will not be willing to forgive" the man who blesses himself in his stubbornness (Deuteronomy 29:20). The Greek word runs from Pilate "wishing to satisfy the crowd" (Mark 15:15) to God "not wishing that any should perish" (2 Peter 3:9). Each passage gives the reason: faith, honour, force, fear, grief, covenant, love, a self-blessing heart. I read the change as following what is refused, and for whose sake (10.7, *Willing*).
- **Planning ahead.** The same looking ahead is a king's honest count of his strength (Luke 14:31) and sailors' guess "on the chance that somehow" (Acts 27:12). It is a man's "aim in life" (2 Timothy 3:10) and a plot "to put him to death" (John 11:53). I read the verses as setting the difference beside how much the planner can see. The king can count, the sailors cannot see the reef, and over all of it "the Lord establishes his steps" (Proverbs 16:9).
- **Reckoning.** People misreckon: "we esteemed him stricken" (Isaiah 53:4). God reckons faith "as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6). The law reckons in order to release (Leviticus 25:50). Love refuses to reckon at all: it "is not … resentful" (1 Corinthians 13:5).
- **Likening.** Comparing is how love praises ("I compare you, my love", Song of Songs 1:9), how comfort reaches out (Lamentations 2:13), and how worship ends ("who in the skies can be compared to the Lord?", Psalm 89:6). It is also how pride rises: "I will make myself like the Most High" (Isaiah 14:14).
- **Reasoning.** The Greek word is Mary's honest pondering (Luke 1:29), the disciples' anxious circling (Mark 8:17), and a quarrel (Philippians 2:14; 1 Timothy 2:8).
- **The nose.** The Hebrew word for anger, *ʾaph*, is the nostril where God breathed in life (Genesis 2:7), the face bowed in worship (2 Chronicles 7:3), and the face lifted in pride (Psalm 10:4). It can be given a ring in love (Ezekiel 16:12) or a hook for raging (2 Kings 19:28). "Long of nostrils" is patience, in God and in the wise (Exodus 34:6; Proverbs 14:29).
- **Anger.** Jesus's anger heals (Mark 3:5). A crowd's anger stops its ears and kills (Acts 7:57–58). "Be angry and do not sin" (Ephesians 4:26).
- **Vexation.** It is provocation done to another (1 Samuel 1:6), suffering borne (1:16), and "Sorrow is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad" (Ecclesiastes 7:3).
- **Provoking.** Love "is not irritable" (1 Corinthians 13:5), with the same word that tells believers to "stir up one another to love and good works" (Hebrews 10:24).
- **Overflow.** One Hebrew word, *ʿebrah*, is the overflow of anger and the overflow of pride. God offers it to Job with irony: "Pour out the overflowings of your anger, and look on everyone who is proud and abase him" (Job 40:11). And "'Scoffer' is the name of the arrogant, haughty man who acts with arrogant pride" (Proverbs 21:24), where the word is the same.
- **Storm.** The same storm word, *sāʿar*, is the angry king's mind ("the mind of the king of Syria was greatly troubled", 2 Kings 6:11) and the suffering city ("O afflicted one, storm-tossed and not comforted", Isaiah 54:11).
- **Denouncing.** "How can I curse whom God has not cursed?" (Numbers 23:8). But "Whoever says to the wicked, 'You are in the right,' will be cursed by peoples, abhorred by nations" (Proverbs 24:24). The word is empty when it goes against God's verdict, and it lands when it follows justice.
- **A creed.** "Slow to anger" is used in worship, in pleading, in confession, in Jonah's complaint, in praise, in wonder, in announcing judgment, and as the ground for returning (Chapter 10.9).
- **Mourning.** Aaron is forbidden to mourn "lest … wrath come" (Leviticus 10:6). When the wrath has come, mourning is commanded (Jeremiah 4:8).
- **God's hand.** The "mighty hand" brought Israel out (Deuteronomy 6:21) and later fought "against you … in anger" (Jeremiah 21:5).
- **Fear.** One word, *yārēʾ*, "to fear", names the fear that drives a person away from God and the fear of God that keeps a person from sin. In one sentence Moses takes the first away and sets the second in its place: "Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin" (Exodus 20:20). The same people, with the same word, are afraid of Egypt and then fear the Lord (Exodus 14:10, 31). Turned round, the word describes the one who is feared: "the great and awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love" (Nehemiah 1:5). Beside a choice it has three more faces. It is learned at a feast in the place God chose: "that you may learn to fear the Lord your God always" (Deuteronomy 14:23). It falls on those who hear of presumption punished: "all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again" (17:13). And it comes as terror on people who resisted God's choice once he made it plain: "Are we all to perish?" (Numbers 17:13). Section 10.1 sets out the word, and 10.7 the faces beside a choice.
- **"Do not fear."** God says it with a reason, and the reason is himself: "for I am with you" (Isaiah 41:10). Joseph says it and refuses to stand in God's place (Genesis 50:19, 21). Jael says it before the tent peg (Judges 4:18). The words are the same. What they are for is not.
- **Trembling and dread.** The Hebrew words for trembling and dread are rendered as fear, and also as "Be angry" (Psalm 4:4), "deeply moved" (2 Samuel 18:33), a heart that "trembled for the ark of God" (1 Samuel 4:13), and "your heart shall thrill and exult" (Isaiah 60:5). I read them as naming one inner stirring, which its situation turns into fear, anger, grief, care or joy (10.1).
- **"None shall make you afraid."** It is promised peace: "I will give peace in the land, and you shall lie down, and none shall make you afraid" (Leviticus 26:6). The same Hebrew phrase is used of desolation: "The cities of Aroer are deserted; they will be for flocks, which will lie down, and none will make them afraid" (Isaiah 17:2). One phrase describes rest for a people and the emptiness left when they are gone.
- **Care.** The Greek *merimnaō*, "to be anxious, to care", is rebuked when it is about my own food and clothing (Matthew 6:25) and praised when it is "genuinely concerned for your welfare" (Philippians 2:20). The Hebrew *dāʾag*, "to be anxious, to dread", is dread of what may come (Jeremiah 38:19), a father's worry for his son (1 Samuel 10:2), and sorrow for sin: "I am sorry for my sin" (Psalm 38:18). Section 10.1 sets this out.
- **Hiding.** The Hebrew *sātar*, "to hide", is God hiding a person in safety and God hiding his face, four verses apart (Psalm 27:5, 9), and a sinner asking God to hide his face from his sins (Psalm 51:9). A treasure is hidden "in his joy", and a talent hidden because "I was afraid" (Matthew 13:44; 25:25). Sections 10.9 and 10.11.
- **Murmuring.** The Hebrew *rāgan* is the people's complaint "in your tents" against God (Deuteronomy 1:27) and the whisperer's words that separate friends (Proverbs 16:28) (10.5).
- **Remembering.** It bows the soul down and it gives hope, in two consecutive verses (Lamentations 3:20–21; Chapter 10.3).
- **The bed.** It is the same place, but what happens there goes either way. "He plots trouble while on his bed" (Psalm 36:4). "I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night" (Psalm 63:6).
- **"Good" or "evil" in your eyes.** Joshua leaves the choice to the people's own sight: "if it is evil in your eyes to serve the Lord, choose this day" (Joshua 24:15). The king honours an old man's sight: "whatever seems good to you" (2 Samuel 19:38). In Isaiah the measure is the Lord's: "you did what was evil in my eyes" (Isaiah 65:12). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Knowing good and evil.** It is the child's knowing "how to refuse the evil and choose the good" (Isaiah 7:15). It is Barzillai's palate at eighty, with the same words: "Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not?" (2 Samuel 19:35). And it is the weighing of words in a dispute: "Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good" (Job 34:4).
- **Refusing.** The Hebrew *māʾas*, "to refuse, reject, despise", is refusing the evil (Isaiah 7:15) and refusing "the waters of Shiloah that flow gently" (8:6). Elihu uses it of refusing God's terms (Job 34:33). Job turns it on himself: "therefore I despise myself, and repent" (42:6).
- **Choosing.** The Hebrew *bāḥar*, "to choose", is the choice of a master (Joshua 24:15), of a place to live (Deuteronomy 23:16), of a way (Psalm 119:30; Isaiah 66:3), of wisdom over silver (Proverbs 16:16), and of a verdict (Job 34:4).
- **Delight.** The Hebrew *ḥāpēṣ*, "to delight in", is the soul's own delight in what it chose: "their soul delights in their abominations" (Isaiah 66:3). It is also the Lord's delight as the measure of a choice. That delight is not met when people "chose what I did not delight in" (65:12), and met in those "who choose the things that please me" (56:4). The noun *ḥēpheṣ* names his settled purpose: "he shall fulfill all my purpose" (Isaiah 44:28). It names what a man cares about, and that stops at his death: "what do they care for their houses after them" (Job 21:21).
- **Good, said of the eye.** "Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor" (Proverbs 22:9). "Bountiful" is literally "good" (10.6).
- **God's delight in a person.** It is the thanks of the rescued: "he rescued me, because he delighted in me" (Psalm 18:19). It is the mockers' taunt over a sufferer: "let him rescue him, for he delights in him!" (Psalm 22:8). The claim is the same. The sufferer does not answer the mockers; he answers God: "Yet you are he who took me from the womb" (22:9) (13.1).
- **An offering.** "For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it" (Psalm 51:16). Three verses on: "then will you delight in right sacrifices, in burnt offerings and whole burnt offerings" (51:19). It is the same offering. Between the two stands "a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (51:17) (13.1).
- **Being well pleased.** The Greek *eudokeō* is the Father's word over the Son: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:17). It is also Paul's word for weaknesses he had pleaded three times to lose: "I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities" (2 Corinthians 12:10). Between his pleading and his contentment stands the answer, "My grace is sufficient for you" (12:9) (10.1).
- **Choosing a person.** God chooses "before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him" (Ephesians 1:4). He chooses people who are "blind, yet have eyes" (Isaiah 43:8, 10), and "those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith" (James 2:5). People choose by what they can already see: "men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom" (Acts 6:3). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Holiness.** It is the purpose of being chosen: "that we should be holy and blameless before him" (Ephesians 1:4). It is also a name the chosen already carry, while the inner qualities are still to be put on: "Put on then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts" (Colossians 3:12). The verses do not say how the two fit.
- **Desire beside a choice.** The soul's desire for meat is given room away from the place God chose: "you may eat within your towns whenever you desire" (Deuteronomy 12:21). The same words for the soul's desire draw a Levite to that place: "he may come when he desires" (18:6). And the soul's delight goes with a wrong choice: "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations" (Isaiah 66:3). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Despising.** Michal "despised him in her heart" when she saw the chosen king dancing before the Lord (2 Samuel 6:16). The same verb describes the servant, "one deeply despised", before whom kings will bow (Isaiah 49:7). People despise the chosen people, judging that God has rejected them (Jeremiah 33:24). And the chosen people themselves "despised the pleasant land" (Psalm 106:24). Each verse gives its own ground: honour before people, a verdict drawn from ruin, no faith in the promise.
- **Knowing that a choice was made.** Peter's hearers know it, and a quarrel ends in silence: "you know that in the early days God made a choice among you" (Acts 15:7, 12). Paul knows it of others from what he saw: "we know … that he has chosen you, because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power" (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5). Cyrus is called for the sake of the chosen "though you do not know me" (Isaiah 45:4). The world hates the chosen "because they do not know him who sent me" (John 15:21).
- **Precious.** The Hebrew *yāqār* is wisdom weighed above *"nothing you desire"* (Proverbs 3:15), the word *"rare in those days"* (1 Samuel 3:1), a visit kept *seldom* (Proverbs 25:17), *"the moon moving in splendor"* that entices a heart (Job 31:26–27), a name *"highly esteemed"* (1 Samuel 18:30), *"the lordly price"* set on a shepherd (Zechariah 11:13), and a son *"dear"* while spoken against (Jeremiah 31:20). The Greek *timios* is faith tested by fire (1 Peter 1:7), the blood of Christ (1:19), and the jewels of Babylon (Revelation 17:4). What differs is who values, what the thing is weighed against, and whether its worth is known: man does not know wisdom's worth (Job 28:13), and Saul would not give the esteem the others gave (1 Samuel 18:29–30). (10.6 *Precious*.)

The Bible's words for anxiety do not all mean the same thing either.
- ***Merimnaō*, "to be anxious, to care".** This is the Greek word for anxiety about food and clothing (Matthew 6:25–34). It is also the word for Paul's "daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches" (2 Corinthians 11:28), for Timothy, who "will be genuinely concerned for your welfare" (Philippians 2:20), and for the members of the body who "have the same care for one another" (1 Corinthians 12:25). The word is not bad in itself. What it is about decides what it is.
- ***Meteōrizō*, "to be held in suspense".** Luke uses it once, in the same teaching: "do not seek what you are to eat and what you are to drink, nor be worried" (Luke 12:29).
- ***Dāʾag*, "to be anxious, to dread", and *deʾāgāh*, "anxiety".** The Hebrew word looks ahead to a harm that may come. The tribes east of the Jordan built their altar "from fear that in time to come your children might say to our children, 'What have you to do with the Lord, the God of Israel?'" (Joshua 22:24). Zedekiah would not surrender: "I am afraid of the Judeans who have deserted to the Chaldeans" (Jeremiah 38:19). And the "dread" of Isaiah 57:11, which led to a lie and to forgetting God (in the fear section above), is this word. Yet the psalmist turns the same word on his own sin: "I confess my iniquity; I am sorry for my sin" (Psalm 38:18).
- ***Śarʿappîm*, "anxious thoughts".** "When the cares of my heart are many, your consolations cheer my soul" (Psalm 94:19). "Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts!" (Psalm 139:23).

section: Fear set against faith and love
paragraph: The word for cowardice stands in two places. In the boat it is Jesus' question, "Why are you afraid, O you of little faith?" (Matthew 8:26). At the end, "the cowardly" head the list of those whose portion is "the second death" (Revelation 21:8).

**The Son's authority.** "All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me" (Matthew 28:18). "that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins" (Matthew 9:6). "he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man" (John 5:27). "you have given him authority over all flesh, to give eternal life to all whom you have given him" (John 17:2). Over his own life: "I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again. This charge I have received from my Father" (John 10:18). He gives it on: "he called to him his twelve disciples and gave them authority over unclean spirits" (Matthew 10:1). He is "the head of all rule and authority" (Colossians 2:10); "He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame" (2:15; 13.3).

The verses follow fear into what the person does next. Some of these lead away from God and from others, and some lead toward them.
- **It hides and keeps away.** "I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself" (Genesis 3:10). At Sinai "the people were afraid and trembled, and they stood far off" (Exodus 20:18). Joseph of Arimathea was a disciple "secretly for fear of the Jews" (John 19:38). The disciples met "the doors being locked … for fear of the Jews" (John 20:19). Section 10.11 follows this.
- **It flees.** Uriah "was afraid and fled and escaped to Egypt" (Jeremiah 26:21).
- **It silences.** "Samuel was afraid to tell the vision to Eli" (1 Samuel 3:15). "Yet for fear of the Jews no one spoke openly of him" (John 7:13). "They did not understand the saying, and were afraid to ask him" (Mark 9:32). Section 10.5 follows this.
- **It bends speech and conduct.** Sarah said she did not laugh, "for she was afraid" (Genesis 18:15). Saul: "I feared the people and obeyed their voice" (1 Samuel 15:24). At Antioch Peter "drew back and separated himself, fearing the circumcision party. And the rest of the Jews acted hypocritically along with him" (Galatians 2:12–13).
- **It holds back the hand, but not the wish.** "The young man did not draw his sword, for he was afraid" (Judges 8:20). The chief priests were "seeking to arrest him", but "they feared the crowds" (Matthew 21:46). Herod "wanted to put him to death", but "he feared the people" (Matthew 14:5). The arrest is not made. The verses do not say the wish has changed.
- **It stops the will.** Saul's armor-bearer "would not, for he feared greatly" (1 Samuel 31:4). "David was afraid of the Lord that day … So David was not willing to take the ark" (2 Samuel 6:9–10). Israel "would not go up" when "Our brothers have made our hearts melt" (Deuteronomy 1:26, 28). In David's case what he heard next moved him again (2 Samuel 6:12). 10.7 (*Willing*) follows the will.
- **It hardens into enmity.** "Saul was even more afraid of David. So Saul was David's enemy continually" (1 Samuel 18:29).
- **It spreads.** The fearful man is sent home "lest he make the heart of his fellows melt like his own" (Deuteronomy 20:8). "Great fear came upon all who heard of it" (Acts 5:5).
- **It turns to God.** "When I am afraid, I put my trust in you" (Psalm 56:3). "Jehoshaphat was afraid and set his face to seek the Lord" (2 Chronicles 20:3). Peter, sinking: "Lord, save me" (Matthew 14:30).
- **It comes forward and tells the truth.** The woman healed of her bleeding, "knowing what had happened to her, came in fear and trembling and fell down before him and told him the whole truth" (Mark 5:33). The jailer, "trembling with fear he fell down before Paul and Silas", asked, "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?" (Acts 16:29–30).
- **It glorifies God, or asks him to go.** "When the crowds saw it, they were afraid, and they glorified God" (Matthew 9:8). But when the Gerasenes saw the healed man, they "asked him to depart from them, for they were seized with great fear" (Luke 8:37). Felix, hearing of "righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment", "was alarmed and said, 'Go away for the present'" (Acts 24:25).
- **It asks a question.** "Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?" (Mark 4:41). "What then will this child be?" (Luke 1:66).

Scripture does speak of people alive before God after death, and it uses both words.
- John sees "under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God", crying out for justice (Revelation 6:9–10).

paragraph:
Fear of other people takes several forms in the verses.
- **Fear of man.** "who are you that you are afraid of man who dies" (Isaiah 51:12). "do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul" (Matthew 10:28).
- **Fear for another.** Eli trembled for the ark (1 Samuel 4:13). Jeremiah grieved for his people: "For the wound of the daughter of my people is my heart wounded; I mourn, and dismay has taken hold on me" (Jeremiah 8:21). Paul: "I am afraid that as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ" (2 Corinthians 11:3).
- **Fear used as a tool.** "he was hired, that I should be afraid and act in this way and sin" (Nehemiah 6:13).
- **Respect owed.** The same word as fear is rendered "respect" toward people. "respect to whom respect is owed, honor to whom honor is owed" (Romans 13:7). "Servants, be subject to your masters with all respect, not only to the good and gentle but also to the unjust" (1 Peter 2:18). Toward parents: "Every one of you shall revere his mother and his father" (Leviticus 19:3).
- **Respect and no fear, two verses apart.** "Have no fear of them, nor be troubled, but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect" (1 Peter 3:14–15). In Greek, "fear" and "respect" are the same word. The verse does not say whether the respect is toward the one who asks or toward God.
- **Being feared.** Being feared works on the one who is feared. "The horror you inspire has deceived you, and the pride of your heart" (Jeremiah 49:16).

paragraph:
The verses show fear changing character, and they point to what changes it.
- **What it is turned toward.** At the sea Israel "feared greatly" as Egypt marched, and after the crossing "the people feared the Lord, and they believed in the Lord" (Exodus 14:10, 31). In between, fear spoke as a preference: "it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness" (14:12; 10.6, *Shaped by fear*). In the boat, fear of the storm became fear of the one who stilled it (Mark 4:41). In these cases the change came after God acted.
- **One fear set in place of another, by the same speaker.** "Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you" (Exodus 20:20). "do not fear what they fear … Let him be your fear" (Isaiah 8:12–13). "Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell", and then, "Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows" (Matthew 10:28, 31).
- **Who speaks to it, and why.** God's "for I am with you" (Isaiah 41:10), and Jael's "do not be afraid" (Judges 4:18).
- **Who meets it.** "When justice is done, it is a joy to the righteous but terror to evildoers" (Proverbs 21:15). One scroll was read aloud: the officials "turned one to another in fear", and "neither the king nor any of his servants who heard all these words was afraid" (Jeremiah 36:16, 24). At the signs of the end, "people fainting with fear", and to the disciples, "straighten up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near" (Luke 21:26, 28).
- **One's own conduct.** "rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad" (Romans 13:3). "I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them, because when I called, no one answered" (Isaiah 66:4). The same passage opens with the one God looks to, who "trembles at my word" (66:2). I read the passage as setting that trembling beside "their fears".
- **Pride.** "So do not become proud, but fear" (Romans 11:20). "The horror you inspire has deceived you, and the pride of your heart" (Jeremiah 49:16).
- **Where the heart is.** Fear "taught by men" while "their hearts are far from me", against fear put "in their hearts" (Isaiah 29:13; Jeremiah 32:40).
- **Faith, trust and love** (the section above).
- **Joy or silence.** The women left the tomb "with fear and great joy, and ran to tell his disciples" (Matthew 28:8). In Mark's account "they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid" (Mark 16:8). The two accounts stand side by side.
- **The same root, rendered as another movement.** *Rāgaz*, "to tremble", is also anger and grief (Psalm 4:4; 2 Samuel 18:33). *Paḥad*, "dread", is also "thrill" (Isaiah 60:5). *Phobos*, "fear", is also "respect" (Romans 13:7).

paragraph: Sometimes a hand comes with the word. "Jesus came and touched them, saying, 'Rise, and have no fear'" (Matthew 17:7). "He laid his right hand on me, saying, 'Fear not'" (Revelation 1:17). When Peter sank, "Jesus immediately reached out his hand and took hold of him" (Matthew 14:31).

**The voice again, on the mountain.** Peter was saying, "Lord, it is good that we are here. If you wish, I will make three tents here", when "a voice from the cloud said, 'This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him'" (Matthew 17:4–5). The words of the baptism come back with a command added. "When the disciples heard this, they fell on their faces and were terrified. But Jesus came and touched them, saying, 'Rise, and have no fear'" (17:6–7). The Father's pleasure, spoken to them, frightens them, and the Son lifts them. Peter recalls it years later as the ground of what he preaches: "we did not follow cleverly devised myths … we ourselves heard this very voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain" (2 Peter 1:16–18), and the word is to be heeded "until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts" (1:19).

In the resurrection, "they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven" (Matthew 22:30). Luke gives the reason: "for they cannot die anymore, because they are equal to angels and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection" (Luke 20:36). "Death shall be no more" (Revelation 21:4).

Jesus speaks of death as sleep. "the girl is not dead but sleeping. And they laughed at him" (Matthew 9:24); Luke adds, "knowing that she was dead" (Luke 8:53). Of Lazarus he says, "Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him." The disciples hear it as rest: "Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover." So "Jesus told them plainly, 'Lazarus has died'" (John 11:11–14). The picture had to be said plainly before they understood it. At his own death, "many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised" (Matthew 27:52).

paragraph: Jesus himself sought to be hidden at times, and could not be. "he entered a house and did not want anyone to know, yet he could not be hidden. But immediately a woman … heard of him and came and fell down at his feet" (Mark 7:24–25). Again, "he did not want anyone to know, for he was teaching his disciples, saying to them, 'The Son of Man is going to be delivered into the hands of men'" (9:30–31).

Jesus himself sought to be hidden at times, and could not be. "he entered a house and did not want anyone to know, yet he could not be hidden. But immediately a woman … heard of him and came and fell down at his feet" (Mark 7:24–25). Again, "he did not want anyone to know, for he was teaching his disciples, saying to them, 'The Son of Man is going to be delivered into the hands of men'" (9:30–31).

**The will asked for.** Jesus asks people what they want.
- To blind men who had cried out against the crowd's rebuke: "What do you want me to do for you?" "Lord, let our eyes be opened." And "Jesus in pity touched their eyes" (Matthew 20:32–34). To Bartimaeus, the same question, and "your faith has made you well" (Mark 10:51–52).
- To a man ill for thirty-eight years: "Do you want to be healed?" He answers with what he lacks: "Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool" (John 5:6–7). He is healed without the pool (5:8).
- To James and John, who came saying "we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you": "What do you want me to do for you?" They asked for the places of honour, and he answered, "You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink?" (Mark 10:35–38; Matthew 20:21–22).
- To the twelve, when many turned back: "Do you want to go away as well?" "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life" (John 6:67–68).
The same question is answered with sight, with a lack, with ambition and with staying. I read the question as drawing the will out into words, where it can be met.

Each party that comes into fear's verses does so in its own way.
- **God** lays dread (Genesis 35:5). He speaks *fear not* with himself as its ground. His acts are named by the terror word: "great deeds of terror, all of which the Lord your God did for you in Egypt before your eyes", "that you might know that the Lord is God" (Deuteronomy 4:34–35). Once he speaks of holding back "had I not feared provocation by the enemy" (Deuteronomy 32:27), and the reason he gives is what the enemy would say.
- **Job names God's terrors as borne in his spirit:** "the arrows of the Almighty are in me; my spirit drinks their poison; the terrors of God are arrayed against me" (Job 6:4).
- **The Holy Spirit** is named with the fear of the Lord: "walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit" (Acts 9:31). On the shoot of Jesse rests "the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the Lord" (Isaiah 11:2).
- **Angels** bring fear and speak against it (Luke 1:12–13; 2:9–10).
- **Other spirits.** A spirit unseen raises dread in the night (Job 4:15). Demons believe and shudder: "You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe—and shudder!" (James 2:19).
- **The physical world** trembles before God in the words used of people. "When the waters saw you, O God, when the waters saw you, they were afraid; indeed, the deep trembled" (Psalm 77:16). The waters also go over a person as God's: "Why are you cast down, O my soul … all your breakers and your waves have gone over me" (Psalm 42:5, 7).
- **Creatures** are made "without fear" (Job 41:33), and dread is laid on them (Genesis 9:2).
- **A loved one** is described by the dread word. The beloved is "awesome as an army with banners" (Song of Songs 6:4).

And none of it is hidden.
- "You discern my thoughts from afar" (Psalm 139:2).
- "The Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought" (1 Chronicles 28:9).
- He knows the inclination before it is acted on: "I know what they are inclined to do even today" (Deuteronomy 31:21).
- Jesus "perceived their thoughts" (Luke 5:22).
- What is hidden will be brought out. Simeon says the child is set for a sign "so that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed" (Luke 2:34–35).

**Whom he is pleased with.** At Jesus' baptism *"the Holy Spirit descended on him in bodily form, like a dove; and a voice came from heaven, 'You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased'"* (Luke 3:22). In one verse the voice from heaven speaks, the Son is named, and the Spirit comes down. Matthew applies Isaiah's *"my beloved with whom my soul is well pleased"* to Jesus (Matthew 12:18; *Choosing*). Paul says that God *"was pleased to reveal his Son to me"* (Galatians 1:16). And of one who turns back: *"my righteous one shall live by faith, and if he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him"* (Hebrews 10:38). Wisdom says that favour is found by finding her: *"For whoever finds me finds life and obtains favor from the Lord, but he who fails to find me injures himself; all who hate me love death"* (Proverbs 8:35–36). The finding is by daily waiting, *"watching daily at my gates, waiting beside my doors"* (8:34). At the end love and hate are turned over: to hate wisdom is to love death, a love the person does not know he has.

**Offered, sought, refused.** "Rule over us … for you have saved us from the hand of Midian." Gideon: "I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; the Lord will rule over you" (Judges 8:22–23). Offered a place as third ruler, Daniel said, "Let your gifts be for yourself, and give your rewards to another. Nevertheless, I will read the writing to the king" (Daniel 5:17). The devil offered all authority for worship, and was refused (Luke 4:6–8; 13.3). Gideon's son sought it through kinship: "Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh", and "their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, 'He is our brother'" (Judges 9:2–3). He then killed his seventy brothers (9:5).

The devil claims a will over what was given into his hand, and seeks worship with it. "To you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been delivered to me, and I give it to whom I will. If you, then, will worship me, it will all be yours." Jesus answered, "You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve" (Luke 4:6–8). People can be held by that will: opponents are to be corrected with gentleness, "God may perhaps grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth, and they may come to their senses and escape from the snare of the devil, after being captured by him to do his will" (2 Timothy 2:25–26).

The English "fear" covers many Hebrew and Greek words, and one word can be rendered many ways.
- ***Yārēʾ*, "to fear".** It is the ordinary word, used for fear of an enemy and for the fear of God. Turned round, it describes the one who is feared: God is "awesome" (Deuteronomy 10:17), and the wilderness is "great and terrifying" (Deuteronomy 1:19). It is also rendered as a way of acting: "One who is wise is cautious and turns away from evil" (Proverbs 14:16).
- ***Paḥad*, "dread".** This is the dread that falls on a person. Once the same verb is used of joy: "your heart shall thrill and exult" (Isaiah 60:5).
- ***Ḥārad*, "to tremble".** The body trembles with it. Yet Eli "was sitting on his seat by the road watching, for his heart trembled for the ark of God" (1 Samuel 4:13).
- ***Rāgaz*, "to tremble, be stirred".** The earth quakes with it. The ESV also renders it "Be angry, and do not sin" (Psalm 4:4), "Do not quarrel on the way" (Genesis 45:24), and David "was deeply moved" and wept for Absalom (2 Samuel 18:33).
- ***Môrāʾ*, "fear, terror".** This is the word of "Let him be your fear, and let him be your dread" (Isaiah 8:13), and of God's "great deeds of terror" in Egypt (Deuteronomy 4:34).
- **The terror and horror words.** *Māgôr*, "terror", gives the name "Terror on Every Side" (Jeremiah 20:3). *Šammâ*, "horror, desolation", names a people as what others are horrified at: "I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth" (Jeremiah 24:9).
- **The Greek words.** *Phobos*, "fear", and its verb carry most of the New Testament verses. The ESV renders the one word as terror, respect, reverence and awe: "rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad"; "respect to whom respect is owed" (Romans 13:3, 7); "submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ" (Ephesians 5:21); "filled with awe" (Luke 5:26). With it go *tromos*, "trembling"; *deilia*, "cowardice"; *eulabeia*, "reverence"; and *ekthambeō*, "to be alarmed".

paragraph:
Fear before a holy act is not one response. The verses set two ends side by side:
- glory and confession: "Fear seized them all, and they glorified God" (Luke 7:16); the centurion, "filled with awe", said, "Truly this was the Son of God!" (Matthew 27:54)
- sending away: "Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord" (Luke 5:8); the Gerasenes (Luke 8:37); Felix (Acts 24:25)

Scripture shows life coming back through each of the inner words.
- **The spirit returns.** Samson, dying of thirst after his victory, drank the water God gave, and "his spirit returned, and he revived" (Judges 15:19). Jairus's daughter: "her spirit returned, and she got up at once" (Luke 8:55). Jesus then tells them to give her something to eat.
- **The life returns.** Elijah prays over the widow's son, and "the life of the child came into him again, and he revived" (1 Kings 17:22). Elisha "restored the dead to life" (2 Kings 8:5). Even after Elisha's death, a dead man thrown into his grave, "as soon as the man touched the bones of Elisha, he revived and stood on his feet" (2 Kings 13:21).
- **The breath enters.** Ezekiel is shown a valley of bones and asked, "Son of man, can these bones live?" He answers, "O Lord God, you know" (Ezekiel 37:3). God's word to the bones builds the body first, then gives the breath: "I will lay sinews upon you, and will cause flesh to come upon you, and cover you with skin, and put breath in you, and you shall live" (37:6). Bones, sinews, flesh and skin come together, "but there was no breath in them" (37:8). When the prophet calls to the breath, "the breath came into them, and they lived and stood on their feet" (37:10). In Revelation, "a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood up on their feet" (Revelation 11:11).

paragraph: Anxiety, as the verses show it, is a mind and heart taken up with something not yet made safe: food and clothing, tomorrow, what to say before a court, other people, one's own sin. Proverbs gives it weight: "Anxiety in a man's heart weighs him down, but a good word makes him glad" (Proverbs 12:25). Jesus names what it is usually about: "do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you will put on" (Matthew 6:25). Here "life" is the life that needs feeding, and Luke's version gives the reason not to be anxious: "For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing" (Luke 12:23).

The verses also name the way out. "Truly, truly, I say to you, an hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live" (John 5:25); "whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me … has passed from death to life" (5:24). God "made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses" (Colossians 2:13). To believers: "Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you" (Ephesians 5:14). The lost son "came to himself" and went home, and his father calls it coming alive (Luke 15:17–24). John gives a sign that it has happened: "We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers" (1 John 3:14). "Made alive", below, follows this.

paragraph:
These are prophetic oracles. Jesus also tells of two men after death, and the one who is buried is aware and speaks:
- "The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side. The rich man also died and was buried, and in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side" (Luke 16:22–23).
- He cries, "I am in anguish in this flame". Abraham answers, "Child, remember that you in your lifetime received your good things … but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish", and "between us and you a great chasm has been fixed" (16:24–26).
- He asks for his five brothers, and is told, "If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead" (16:28–31).

Luke gives the reason: "for they cannot die anymore, because they are equal to angels and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection" (Luke 20:36). "Death shall be no more" (Revelation 21:4).

**Planning together, and parting.** Plans are often made with others, and others may not agree.
- Paul and Barnabas planned to revisit the churches. *"Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark. But Paul thought best not to take with them one who had withdrawn from them"* (Acts 15:37–38). Each weighed the same past differently, and *"there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other"* (15:39).
- Joseph of Arimathea sat in the council that sent Jesus to death, but he *"had not consented to their decision and action"* (Luke 23:51). He did not share their plan, and the next verse shows him acting on his own: *"This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus"* (23:52).

section: Flesh in the New Testament: one word, several values
paragraph:
- "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:14).
- "In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears" (Hebrews 5:7).
- "The life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God" (Galatians 2:20).
- "If I am to live in the flesh, that means fruitful labor for me" (Philippians 1:22).
- "A thorn was given me in the flesh" (2 Corinthians 12:7).

**The will asked for.** Jesus asks people what they want.
- To blind men who had cried out against the crowd's rebuke: "What do you want me to do for you?" "Lord, let our eyes be opened." And "Jesus in pity touched their eyes" (Matthew 20:32–34). To Bartimaeus, the same question, and "your faith has made you well" (Mark 10:51–52).
- To a man ill for thirty-eight years: "Do you want to be healed?" He answers with what he lacks: "Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool" (John 5:6–7). He is healed without the pool (5:8).
- To James and John, who came saying "we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you": "What do you want me to do for you?" They asked for the places of honour, and he answered, "You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink?" (Mark 10:35–38; Matthew 20:21–22).
- To the twelve, when many turned back: "Do you want to go away as well?" "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life" (John 6:67–68).
The same question is answered with sight, with a lack, with ambition and with staying. I read the question as drawing the will out into words, where it can be met.

In the New Testament, giving life belongs to the Father, to the Son and to the Spirit.
- "For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will" (John 5:21).
- Abraham believed "God … who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist" (Romans 4:17).
- "It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life" (John 6:63).
- "For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life" (2 Corinthians 3:6).

paragraph:
**The Father's will, the Son's choosing, the Spirit's willing.**
- *"yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. All things have been handed over to me by my Father … and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him"* (Matthew 11:26–27). Luke adds that Jesus said it as *"he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit"* (Luke 10:21–22). The word for the Son's choosing is the will word.
- The Spirit gives gifts *"to each one individually as he wills"* (1 Corinthians 12:11).
- The Son gives life: *"For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will"* (John 5:21).
- Over a disciple's life: *"If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!"* (John 21:22). The saying was misread at once: *"So the saying spread abroad among the brothers that this disciple was not to die"* (21:23). What it meant for Peter is in 10.7 (*Willing*).

paragraph: The rising is not to life for all. "An hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment" (John 5:28–29). Daniel had been told it: "many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt" (Daniel 12:2). Paul states his hope "that there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust" (Acts 24:15).

section: Delivered from the wrath to come
paragraph: Jesus speaks of a rising that ends in judgment: "those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment" (John 5:29). Daniel was told that some "shall awake … to shame and everlasting contempt" (Daniel 12:2). Chapter 2 (*The body raised*) sets these beside the resurrection of life. Revelation names "the second death", and its list opens with "the cowardly, the faithless" (Revelation 21:8).

**Refusing God refuses something good.** The passages say what was offered:
- the land: *"It is a good land"* (Deuteronomy 1:25), and *"Yet you would not go up"* (1:26)
- rest: *"This is rest; give rest to the weary; and this is repose"; yet they would not hear* (Isaiah 28:12); and *"ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is; and walk in it, and find rest for your souls. But they said, 'We will not walk in it'"* (Jeremiah 6:16)
- the one who brought God's word: *"He received living oracles to give to us. Our fathers refused to obey him, but thrust him aside, and in their hearts they turned to Egypt"* (Acts 7:38–39)
- being filled: *"Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it." But … Israel would not submit to me* (Psalm 81:10–11)
- his Spirit and his words: *"If you turn at my reproof, behold, I will pour out my spirit to you"* (Proverbs 1:23)
- life itself, from the one who gives it: *"yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life"* (John 5:40). Here the passage says what lies behind the refusal. They had searched the Scriptures (5:39), so it was not that they did not know. *"But I know that you do not have the love of God within you … How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?"* (5:42, 44). The will refused because the desire was set on glory from people.
- being gathered: "How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!" (Matthew 23:37; Luke 13:34). His will and theirs stand in one verb (13.1).
- a light received only for a while: "He was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light" (John 5:35)

**At Gethsemane the Son's will is given up to the Father's.** *"Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done." And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him. And being in agony he prayed more earnestly* (Luke 22:42–44). Two wills are named side by side here, and one is given up to the other. John has the Son say it beforehand, as the reason he came: *"For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me. And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day. For this is the will of my Father, that everyone who looks on the Son and believes in him should have eternal life"* (John 6:38–40). The Father's will there has content: that none be lost. What it means for a person's own will is in 10.7 (*Willing*).

And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him. And being in agony he prayed more earnestly* (Luke 22:42–44). Two wills are named side by side here, and one is given up to the other. And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day. For this is the will of my Father, that everyone who looks on the Son and believes in him should have eternal life"* (John 6:38–40). The Father's will there has content: that none be lost. What it means for a person's own will is in 10.7 (*Willing*).

section: Flesh in the New Testament: one word, several values
paragraph: The same word can change value within a single speech. In John 6, Jesus says, "the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh" (6:51), and "whoever feeds on my flesh … has eternal life" (6:54). When the disciples take offence, he says, "It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life" (6:63). Within a dozen verses, flesh is the gift of life and "no help at all".

At the feast the offer is made aloud, and the water now flows outward: *"Jesus stood up and cried out, 'If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.'"* John adds, *"Now this he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive"* (John 7:37–39; Chapter 6). At the well the spring wells up *"in him"*. At the feast rivers flow *"out of his heart"*. I read a want that is met and then becomes a source for others.

And Scripture names life itself as a person. Moses says of the Lord, "he is your life and length of days" (Deuteronomy 30:20). Paul speaks of "Christ who is your life" (Colossians 3:4). At Lazarus's grave Jesus says it of himself: "I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live" (John 11:25). Jesus says where his own life comes from, and where his people's comes from: "For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself" (John 5:26); "Because I live, you also will live" (John 14:19). And he says what life is: "this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent" (John 17:3).

Wanting can be aimed at seeing Jesus, and the verses show it ending in different places. Greeks "came to Philip … and asked him, 'Sir, we wish to see Jesus'", and Jesus answered, "The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified" (John 12:21, 23). Herod "was very glad, for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard about him, and he was hoping to see some sign", and "he made no answer" (Luke 23:8–9). His mother and brothers stood outside "desiring to see you", and he said, "My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it" (8:20–21).

**The Son's will, in its own words.**
- **"I will; be clean."** To the leper who said "If you will, you can make me clean", Jesus, "moved with pity, … stretched out his hand and touched him and said to him, 'I will; be clean'" (Mark 1:40–41; Matthew 8:2–3; Luke 5:12–13). His will and his pity are named together, and his hand touches before he speaks.
- **A gathering refused.** "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!" (Matthew 23:37; Luke 13:34). Then: "your house is left to you desolate", and the door left open, "until you say, 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord'" (Matthew 23:38–39).
- **A longing joined with distress.** "I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled! I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished!" (Luke 12:49–50).
- **For those given him.** "Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory that you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world" (John 17:24).
- **In a parable, the owner's will against the begrudging eye.** "I choose to give to this last worker as I give to you. Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Or do you begrudge my generosity?" (Matthew 20:14–15). *Do you begrudge* is literally *is your eye evil*, the opposite of the good eye that shares its bread (Proverbs 22:9; 10.6).

Where the feeling is named, it is fear.
- Jacob fled from Laban "secretly", and he said why: "Because I was afraid" (Genesis 31:27, 31).
- Isaac hid that Rebekah was his wife, and gave the reason: "Because I thought, 'Lest I die because of her.'" (Genesis 26:9). The fear there is the fear of dying (Chapter 2).
- Joseph of Arimathea was "a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews". The same verse ends with him going to Pilate and taking away the body (John 19:38).

The verses follow fear into what the person does next. Some of these lead away from God and from others, and some lead toward them.
- **It hides and keeps away.** "I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself" (Genesis 3:10). At Sinai "the people were afraid and trembled, and they stood far off" (Exodus 20:18). Joseph of Arimathea was a disciple "secretly for fear of the Jews" (John 19:38). The disciples met "the doors being locked … for fear of the Jews" (John 20:19). Section 10.11 follows this.
- **It flees.** Uriah "was afraid and fled and escaped to Egypt" (Jeremiah 26:21).
- **It silences.** "Samuel was afraid to tell the vision to Eli" (1 Samuel 3:15). "Yet for fear of the Jews no one spoke openly of him" (John 7:13). "They did not understand the saying, and were afraid to ask him" (Mark 9:32). Section 10.5 follows this.
- **It bends speech and conduct.** Sarah said she did not laugh, "for she was afraid" (Genesis 18:15). Saul: "I feared the people and obeyed their voice" (1 Samuel 15:24). At Antioch Peter "drew back and separated himself, fearing the circumcision party. And the rest of the Jews acted hypocritically along with him" (Galatians 2:12–13).
- **It holds back the hand, but not the wish.** "The young man did not draw his sword, for he was afraid" (Judges 8:20). The chief priests were "seeking to arrest him", but "they feared the crowds" (Matthew 21:46). Herod "wanted to put him to death", but "he feared the people" (Matthew 14:5). The arrest is not made. The verses do not say the wish has changed.
- **It stops the will.** Saul's armor-bearer "would not, for he feared greatly" (1 Samuel 31:4). "David was afraid of the Lord that day … So David was not willing to take the ark" (2 Samuel 6:9–10). Israel "would not go up" when "Our brothers have made our hearts melt" (Deuteronomy 1:26, 28). In David's case what he heard next moved him again (2 Samuel 6:12). 10.7 (*Willing*) follows the will.
- **It hardens into enmity.** "Saul was even more afraid of David. So Saul was David's enemy continually" (1 Samuel 18:29).
- **It spreads.** The fearful man is sent home "lest he make the heart of his fellows melt like his own" (Deuteronomy 20:8). "Great fear came upon all who heard of it" (Acts 5:5).
- **It turns to God.** "When I am afraid, I put my trust in you" (Psalm 56:3). "Jehoshaphat was afraid and set his face to seek the Lord" (2 Chronicles 20:3). Peter, sinking: "Lord, save me" (Matthew 14:30).
- **It comes forward and tells the truth.** The woman healed of her bleeding, "knowing what had happened to her, came in fear and trembling and fell down before him and told him the whole truth" (Mark 5:33). The jailer, "trembling with fear he fell down before Paul and Silas", asked, "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?" (Acts 16:29–30).
- **It glorifies God, or asks him to go.** "When the crowds saw it, they were afraid, and they glorified God" (Matthew 9:8). But when the Gerasenes saw the healed man, they "asked him to depart from them, for they were seized with great fear" (Luke 8:37). Felix, hearing of "righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment", "was alarmed and said, 'Go away for the present'" (Acts 24:25).
- **It asks a question.** "Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?" (Mark 4:41). "What then will this child be?" (Luke 1:66).

Scripture speaks of the death of the upright in its own words:
- precious: "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints" (Psalm 116:15)
- wished for: Balaam says, "Let me die the death of the upright, and let my end be like his!" (Numbers 23:10)
- a refuge: "The righteous finds refuge in his death" (Proverbs 14:32)
- in faith: "These all died in faith, not having received the things promised" (Hebrews 11:13); of Abel, "through his faith, though he died, he still speaks" (Hebrews 11:4)
- bearing fruit: "unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit" (John 12:24)
- glorifying God: Jesus speaks to Peter of "what kind of death he was to glorify God" (John 21:19)

paragraph: "But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20). "For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive. But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ" (15:22–23). He is "the firstborn from the dead" (Colossians 1:18). "God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power" (1 Corinthians 6:14). Peter says death could not keep him: "God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it" (Acts 2:24). He and Paul read the psalm of him: "For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, or let your Holy One see corruption" (Acts 2:27). "For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption, but he whom God raised up did not see corruption" (Acts 13:36–37).

section: Soul, spirit and heart at death
paragraph:
**The soul.**
- **It departs.** "As her soul was departing (for she was dying), she called his name Ben-oni" (Genesis 35:18).
- **It dies.** Balaam: "Let me die the death of the upright, and let my end be like his!" (Numbers 23:10). Samson: "Let me die with the Philistines" (Judges 16:30). In both, the Hebrew is *let my soul die*. And "the soul who sins shall die" (Ezekiel 18:4).
- **It is poured out.** Of the servant: "he poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors" (Isaiah 53:12). Before his death Jesus said, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death" (Matthew 26:38).
- **It is named to the very end.** Even the corpse is *nephesh* ("soul"): "Whoever touches the dead body of any person" (Numbers 19:11).
- **It has an end beyond death, and Psalm 49 names two.** The psalm is about the death that comes to everyone: "even the wise die; the fool and the stupid alike must perish" (Psalm 49:10). Of the man who trusts in his wealth: "his soul will go to the generation of his fathers, who will never again see light" (49:19). Of himself, the psalmist says: "But God will ransom my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me" (49:15). The psalm does not say what being received involves, and I do not fill it in. Of those who trust in their wealth it says, "death shall be their shepherd, and the upright shall rule over them in the morning" (49:14), and it draws a word for the living from this: "Be not afraid when a man becomes rich" (49:16).
- **It is not abandoned.** David wrote, "you will not abandon my soul to Sheol, or let your holy one see corruption" (Psalm 16:10). Peter reads it of Christ's death and rising: "he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption" (Acts 2:31).

Corrected 2026-10-04 (#1950): of 15 soul-delivered verses, 12 are rescue from dying; Psa 49:15 (set against the death of all, 49:10) and Psa 16:10 (as Act 2:27, 31 read it) look beyond death; Psa 89:48 says no one can. The verdict holds: no verse gives soul and spirit different destinations. The verses that name Sheol or Hades speak of the soul and never of the spirit. Ecc 3:21 leaves the spirit's destination open ("Who knows?"). section: Lines that are often drawn, but that I cannot find
paragraph: **"The soul goes to Sheol; the spirit goes to God."** The verses usually cited speak of the soul being *delivered from* Sheol ("you will not abandon my soul to Sheol", Psalm 16:10; "you have brought up my soul from Sheol", Psalm 30:3). Psalm 30:3 is about a living person rescued from death. Peter reads Psalm 16:10 of Christ, "not abandoned to Hades" (Acts 2:31). Neither sends the soul one way and the spirit another, and the verses that name Sheol or Hades speak of the soul and never of the spirit. And Ecclesiastes leaves the spirit's destination as a question: "Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward?" (Ecclesiastes 3:21). See Chapter 2.
