paragraph: It can be roused by another's following. After the sick were healed, *"the high priest rose up, and all who were with him … and filled with jealousy they arrested the apostles and put them in the public prison"* (Acts 5:17–18). At Antioch, *"when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and began to contradict what was spoken by Paul, reviling him"* (13:45). Both times it is at a crowd that has come to someone else, and both times they are "filled" with it. In Jerusalem it turns to arrest, in Antioch to speech (10.5).

What follows the anger is where the cases differ. The verses follow it into what the person does.
- **The hand acts at once.** Moses "threw the tablets out of his hands and broke them" (Exodus 32:19). Balaam "struck the donkey with his staff" (Numbers 22:27).
- **Where there is power, a command.** Pharaoh "put them in custody" (Genesis 40:3). Nebuchadnezzar "commanded that all the wise men of Babylon be destroyed" (Daniel 2:12). Herod "sent and killed all the male children in Bethlehem" (Matthew 2:16). "A king's wrath is like the growling of a lion" (Proverbs 19:12).
- **Killing.** "For in their anger they killed men" (Genesis 49:6). God asked Cain, "Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen?" (Genesis 4:6), and Cain "rose up against his brother Abel and killed him" (4:8).
- **A watching eye, and a plot.** "And Saul eyed David from that day on" (1 Samuel 18:9). Sanballat and Tobiah "all plotted together" (Nehemiah 4:8). "The wicked plots against the righteous and gnashes his teeth at him" (Psalm 37:12).
- **Rage that wants to kill at once.** The council heard the apostles and "were enraged and wanted to kill them" (Acts 5:33). This is not a plan laid in advance: the wish follows the rage straight away. Gamaliel, "a teacher of the law held in honor by all the people", stopped it by having the men put outside for a little while: "take care what you are about to do with these men" (5:34–35). Plotting is in 10.10.
- **The face falls, and the body withdraws.** Cain's face fell (Genesis 4:5). Jonathan "ate no food the second day of the month" (1 Samuel 20:34).
- **Counsel, and then a charge.** Nehemiah: "I took counsel with myself, and I brought charges against the nobles" (Nehemiah 5:7).
- **Silence, and waiting.** Absalom "spoke to Amnon neither good nor bad" (2 Samuel 13:22). Two years later he had him killed.
- **Prayer.** "And Samuel was angry, and he cried to the Lord all night" (1 Samuel 15:11). The verses give what was behind it: Saul and the people "spared Agag and the best … and would not utterly destroy them" (15:9), and God said, "he has turned back from following me" (15:11).
- **Fear.** After Uzzah was struck, David was angry, and "David was afraid of the Lord that day" (2 Samuel 6:9).
- **Speech that must come out.** Elihu, angry and long silent: "I must speak, that I may find relief" (Job 32:20). Moses at Meribah: "they made his spirit bitter, and he spoke rashly with his lips" (Psalm 106:33).
- **Mercy.** Saul, after the Spirit came on him in anger and the victory was won, said, "Not a man shall be put to death this day" (1 Samuel 11:13).
- **Staying outside.** The elder brother "refused to go in" (Luke 15:28).
- **Strife.** "A hot-tempered man stirs up strife" (Proverbs 15:18). "One given to anger causes much transgression" (Proverbs 29:22).
- **Separation.** Paul and Barnabas: "there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other" (Acts 15:39).

The verses show anger changing character with its circumstances.
- **Who is angry.** The same words are used for God and for people, and "for I am God and not a man" (Hosea 11:9) is said in restraint.
- **Whether what sets it off is true.** Potiphar acted on a lie (Genesis 39:19).
- **For whom it burns.** For the widow and fatherless (Exodus 22:24); for the children (Mark 10:14); for one wronged (2 Samuel 12:5).
- **What it is joined with in the verse.** Jealousy (Deuteronomy 6:15); grief, "with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart" (Mark 3:5); the Spirit (1 Samuel 11:6); hatred, "the anger and envy that you showed because of your hatred" (Ezekiel 35:11); fear, "he shall be afraid and withdraw, and shall turn back and be enraged" (Daniel 11:30); compassion set against it (Hosea 11:8–9).
- **Time.** God's "for a moment" (Psalm 30:5) and "finished" (Revelation 15:1); a man's wrath kept "forever" (Amos 1:11); "do not let the sun go down on your anger" (Ephesians 4:26).
- **Power.** The ruler's anger becomes a command (Daniel 2:12).
- **The one who carries it out,** and their own heart (Isaiah 10:7).
- **One and many** (Numbers 16:22; Joshua 7:1).
- **What meets it.** A soft answer, a servants' question, a father who comes out, a counsellor (Proverbs 15:1; 2 Kings 5:13; Luke 15:28; Acts 5:34–35). Or no one: "I looked, but there was no one to help" (Isaiah 63:5).
- **Correction with or without the anger:** "Correct me, O Lord, but in justice; not in your anger" (Jeremiah 10:24).
- **The measure:** "storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath" (Romans 2:5).
- **The same root, rendered as another movement.** *ʿEbrāh* is wrath and pride (Proverbs 21:24). *Kāʿas* is provoking God and Hannah's grief (1 Samuel 1:16). *Ḥēmāh* is wrath and venom (Psalm 140:3). *Paroxysmos* is a sharp disagreement and stirring up to love (Acts 15:39; Hebrews 10:24). *Thymos* is God's wrath and Babylon's passion (Revelation 14:8, 10).

When people choose a person, the order is the other way. The gathering in Jerusalem was told to *"pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom"* (Acts 6:3), and they chose Stephen, *"a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit"* (6:5). They chose by what was already seen in him. It was seen in him to the end: *"full of the Holy Spirit"*, he prayed for those who stoned him, *"Lord, do not hold this sin against them"* (7:55, 60).

section: Other ways Scripture shows the inner life
paragraph: Sometimes the inner word in the verse belongs not to the angry person but to someone else. When Jesus is angry, the heart named is his opponents': "grieved at their hardness of heart" (Mark 3:5). While their enemies rage, the builders "had a mind to work" (Nehemiah 4:6). Beside the council's fury, Stephen is "full of the Holy Spirit" (Acts 7:55).

The Gospels show his risen body. They do not define it.
- **He could be touched, and he ate.** When the disciples "thought they saw a spirit", he said, "See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have" (Luke 24:37, 39). They gave him broiled fish, "and he took it and ate before them" (24:42–43). The apostles "ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead" (Acts 10:41). To Thomas he said, "put out your hand, and place it in my side" (John 20:27).
- **He came and went.** With "the doors being locked … Jesus came and stood among them" (John 20:19). At Emmaus "their eyes were opened, and they recognized him. And he vanished from their sight" (Luke 24:31).
- **He was not known at once.** On the road, "their eyes were kept from recognizing him" (Luke 24:16). Mary "saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus" (John 20:14). At the lake, "the disciples did not know that it was Jesus" (21:4).

The new life is life with the Spirit. "For the law of the Spirit of life has set you free in Christ Jesus from the law of sin and death" (Romans 8:2). "Although the body is dead because of sin, the Spirit is life because of righteousness" (Romans 8:10). "If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit" (Galatians 5:25). Repentance itself is given toward life: "Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life" (Acts 11:18). And the life is had now: "Whoever has the Son has life" (1 John 5:12). Chapter 2 ("Made alive") gives the account.

**What he delights in.**
- *"Those of crooked heart are an abomination to the Lord, but those of blameless ways are his delight"* (Proverbs 11:20).
- David, as he gives freely: *"I know, my God, that you test the heart and have pleasure in uprightness"* (1 Chronicles 29:17).
- A purpose in a heart pleases him even when he does not let it be carried out: *"Whereas it was in your heart to build a house for my name, you did well that it was in your heart. Nevertheless, you shall not build the house"* (1 Kings 8:18–19; 2 Chronicles 6:8–9).
- He *"found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart, who will do all my will"* (Acts 13:22).
- To Jehu: *"Because you have done well in carrying out what is right in my eyes, and have done to the house of Ahab according to all that was in my heart, your sons of the fourth generation shall sit on the throne of Israel"* (2 Kings 10:30). The next verse turns to Jehu's own heart: *"But Jehu was not careful to walk in the law of the Lord, the God of Israel, with all his heart"* (10:31).
- A people valued: *"Because you are precious in my eyes, and honored, and I love you, I give men in return for you, peoples in exchange for your life"* (Isaiah 43:4). Hezekiah, delivered, says, *"in love you have delivered my life from the pit of destruction, for you have cast all my sins behind your back"* (Isaiah 38:17).
- A son held dear while spoken against. Ephraim grieves: *"after I had turned away, I relented, and after I was instructed, I struck my thigh; I was ashamed, and I was confounded, because I bore the disgrace of my youth"* (Jeremiah 31:19). God answers: *"Is Ephraim my dear son? Is he my darling child? For as often as I speak against him, I do remember him still. Therefore my heart yearns for him; I will surely have mercy on him, declares the Lord"* (31:20). Speaking against him and remembering him go on together, and the yearning is given as the reason for mercy (10.3, 10.13).
- A price paid: *"you were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from your forefathers, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot"* (1 Peter 1:18–19). Isaiah speaks of men given in exchange for a people precious in his eyes (above). Peter names the price as the blood of Christ, and what it ransoms from as ways inherited.
- A fast he does not accept: *"Will you call this a fast, and a day acceptable to the Lord?"* (Isaiah 58:5). What he chooses instead is in *Choosing* (58:6).
- What his anger gives way to: *"He does not retain his anger forever, because he delights in steadfast love"* (Micah 7:18). The reason the anger ends is what he delights in. Isaiah puts wrath and favour in one sentence: *"for in my wrath I struck you, but in my favor I have had mercy on you"* (Isaiah 60:10), as *"his favor is for a lifetime"* (Psalm 30:5; 10.13).

"But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20). "For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive. But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ" (15:22–23). He is "the firstborn from the dead" (Colossians 1:18). "God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power" (1 Corinthians 6:14). Peter says death could not keep him: "God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it" (Acts 2:24). He and Paul read the psalm of him: "For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, or let your Holy One see corruption" (Acts 2:27). "For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption, but he whom God raised up did not see corruption" (Acts 13:36–37).

In these verses a person's choice is not the first move. It is made in front of a God who has already acted.
- At Shechem the choice comes after eleven verses of what the Lord did, beginning *"I took your father Abraham from beyond the River"* (Joshua 24:3).
- In Isaiah 65 the wrong choice is made in front of a God who says *"Here I am, here I am"* and *"I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people"* (65:1–2).
- At the council in Jerusalem the church's choosing follows Peter's word that *"God made a choice among you"* (Acts 15:7), in the same verb.

**Knowing that a choice was made, and not knowing.** Knowing of a choice can settle a quarrel. In the dispute at Jerusalem, Peter appeals to what they all know: *"you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe"* (Acts 15:7). The purpose of God's choosing one man lay in others, that they would hear and believe, and their hearts were *"cleansed … by faith"* (15:9). The debate falls silent (15:12). Paul knows that the Thessalonians are chosen from what he saw happen: *"because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction"* (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5).

- **A tender heart.** It melts before an enemy and spreads fear to others (Deuteronomy 20:8). But Josiah's heart "was penitent [tender]" before God's word, and God answered him with peace (2 Kings 22:19–20). The same softness is cowardice in one place and repentance in the other.
- **A strong heart.** "Be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the Lord!" (Psalm 27:14). With Absalom, the same verb gives his servants the nerve to kill: "be courageous and be valiant" (2 Samuel 13:28). With Pharaoh it is hardening: "I will harden his heart" (Exodus 4:21), literally *strengthen*.
- **A guarded heart.** "Keep your heart with all vigilance" (Proverbs 4:23). Three chapters later the same word describes the adulteress, "wily [guarded] of heart" (Proverbs 7:10).
- **Crushing.** Crushed by an enemy, the spirit collapses (Psalm 143:3–4). Offered to God, a crushed spirit is the very sacrifice he wants: "a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (Psalm 51:17).
- **Loving and hating one's own soul** (Chapter 5).
- **Devising.** The same Hebrew verb describes the craftsmen who worked cherubim "skillfully" into the tabernacle curtains (Exodus 26:1) and those who plot. One word for planning means "discretion" (Proverbs 2:11), "evil devices" (Proverbs 12:2), and God's own purpose: "no purpose of yours can be thwarted" (Job 42:2).
- **Planning against.** God says, "I am … devising a plan against you. Return" (Jeremiah 18:11), and the people say, "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah" (18:18). The word and the "against" are the same. One plan is meant to bring people back, and the other is meant to silence the one who calls them.
- **Purposing.** The verb for purposing (*zāmam*) is the psalmist's resolve: "I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress" (Psalm 17:3). It is the wicked man's plot: "The wicked plots against the righteous" (Psalm 37:12). It is the wise woman's weighing: "She considers a field and buys it" (Proverbs 31:16). And it is God's fixed purpose: "I have purposed; I have not relented" (Jeremiah 4:28). I read the change as following whom it is aimed at: one's own mouth, another's harm, one's own household, or a whole land.
- **Willing.** The Hebrew word for being willing (*ʾāḇâ*) is almost always a "no". It is the guard's refusal to kill the priests (1 Samuel 22:17), David refusing the water for the men's sake (2 Samuel 23:17), Amnon refusing Tamar's plea (2 Samuel 13:14), and Israel refusing God's rest (Isaiah 30:15). God himself is "not willing to destroy" (2 Kings 8:19), and "will not be willing to forgive" the man who blesses himself in his stubbornness (Deuteronomy 29:20). The Greek word runs from Pilate "wishing to satisfy the crowd" (Mark 15:15) to God "not wishing that any should perish" (2 Peter 3:9). Each passage gives the reason: faith, honour, force, fear, grief, covenant, love, a self-blessing heart. I read the change as following what is refused, and for whose sake (10.7, *Willing*).
- **Planning ahead.** The same looking ahead is a king's honest count of his strength (Luke 14:31) and sailors' guess "on the chance that somehow" (Acts 27:12). It is a man's "aim in life" (2 Timothy 3:10) and a plot "to put him to death" (John 11:53). I read the verses as setting the difference beside how much the planner can see. The king can count, the sailors cannot see the reef, and over all of it "the Lord establishes his steps" (Proverbs 16:9).
- **Reckoning.** People misreckon: "we esteemed him stricken" (Isaiah 53:4). God reckons faith "as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6). The law reckons in order to release (Leviticus 25:50). Love refuses to reckon at all: it "is not … resentful" (1 Corinthians 13:5).
- **Likening.** Comparing is how love praises ("I compare you, my love", Song of Songs 1:9), how comfort reaches out (Lamentations 2:13), and how worship ends ("who in the skies can be compared to the Lord?", Psalm 89:6). It is also how pride rises: "I will make myself like the Most High" (Isaiah 14:14).
- **Reasoning.** The Greek word is Mary's honest pondering (Luke 1:29), the disciples' anxious circling (Mark 8:17), and a quarrel (Philippians 2:14; 1 Timothy 2:8).
- **The nose.** The Hebrew word for anger, *ʾaph*, is the nostril where God breathed in life (Genesis 2:7), the face bowed in worship (2 Chronicles 7:3), and the face lifted in pride (Psalm 10:4). It can be given a ring in love (Ezekiel 16:12) or a hook for raging (2 Kings 19:28). "Long of nostrils" is patience, in God and in the wise (Exodus 34:6; Proverbs 14:29).
- **Anger.** Jesus's anger heals (Mark 3:5). A crowd's anger stops its ears and kills (Acts 7:57–58). "Be angry and do not sin" (Ephesians 4:26).
- **Vexation.** It is provocation done to another (1 Samuel 1:6), suffering borne (1:16), and "Sorrow is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad" (Ecclesiastes 7:3).
- **Provoking.** Love "is not irritable" (1 Corinthians 13:5), with the same word that tells believers to "stir up one another to love and good works" (Hebrews 10:24).
- **Overflow.** One Hebrew word, *ʿebrah*, is the overflow of anger and the overflow of pride. God offers it to Job with irony: "Pour out the overflowings of your anger, and look on everyone who is proud and abase him" (Job 40:11). And "'Scoffer' is the name of the arrogant, haughty man who acts with arrogant pride" (Proverbs 21:24), where the word is the same.
- **Storm.** The same storm word, *sāʿar*, is the angry king's mind ("the mind of the king of Syria was greatly troubled", 2 Kings 6:11) and the suffering city ("O afflicted one, storm-tossed and not comforted", Isaiah 54:11).
- **Denouncing.** "How can I curse whom God has not cursed?" (Numbers 23:8). But "Whoever says to the wicked, 'You are in the right,' will be cursed by peoples, abhorred by nations" (Proverbs 24:24). The word is empty when it goes against God's verdict, and it lands when it follows justice.
- **A creed.** "Slow to anger" is used in worship, in pleading, in confession, in Jonah's complaint, in praise, in wonder, in announcing judgment, and as the ground for returning (Chapter 10.9).
- **Mourning.** Aaron is forbidden to mourn "lest … wrath come" (Leviticus 10:6). When the wrath has come, mourning is commanded (Jeremiah 4:8).
- **God's hand.** The "mighty hand" brought Israel out (Deuteronomy 6:21) and later fought "against you … in anger" (Jeremiah 21:5).
- **Fear.** One word, *yārēʾ*, "to fear", names the fear that drives a person away from God and the fear of God that keeps a person from sin. In one sentence Moses takes the first away and sets the second in its place: "Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin" (Exodus 20:20). The same people, with the same word, are afraid of Egypt and then fear the Lord (Exodus 14:10, 31). Turned round, the word describes the one who is feared: "the great and awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love" (Nehemiah 1:5). Beside a choice it has three more faces. It is learned at a feast in the place God chose: "that you may learn to fear the Lord your God always" (Deuteronomy 14:23). It falls on those who hear of presumption punished: "all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again" (17:13). And it comes as terror on people who resisted God's choice once he made it plain: "Are we all to perish?" (Numbers 17:13). Section 10.1 sets out the word, and 10.7 the faces beside a choice.
- **"Do not fear."** God says it with a reason, and the reason is himself: "for I am with you" (Isaiah 41:10). Joseph says it and refuses to stand in God's place (Genesis 50:19, 21). Jael says it before the tent peg (Judges 4:18). The words are the same. What they are for is not.
- **Trembling and dread.** The Hebrew words for trembling and dread are rendered as fear, and also as "Be angry" (Psalm 4:4), "deeply moved" (2 Samuel 18:33), a heart that "trembled for the ark of God" (1 Samuel 4:13), and "your heart shall thrill and exult" (Isaiah 60:5). I read them as naming one inner stirring, which its situation turns into fear, anger, grief, care or joy (10.1).
- **"None shall make you afraid."** It is promised peace: "I will give peace in the land, and you shall lie down, and none shall make you afraid" (Leviticus 26:6). The same Hebrew phrase is used of desolation: "The cities of Aroer are deserted; they will be for flocks, which will lie down, and none will make them afraid" (Isaiah 17:2). One phrase describes rest for a people and the emptiness left when they are gone.
- **Care.** The Greek *merimnaō*, "to be anxious, to care", is rebuked when it is about my own food and clothing (Matthew 6:25) and praised when it is "genuinely concerned for your welfare" (Philippians 2:20). The Hebrew *dāʾag*, "to be anxious, to dread", is dread of what may come (Jeremiah 38:19), a father's worry for his son (1 Samuel 10:2), and sorrow for sin: "I am sorry for my sin" (Psalm 38:18). Section 10.1 sets this out.
- **Hiding.** The Hebrew *sātar*, "to hide", is God hiding a person in safety and God hiding his face, four verses apart (Psalm 27:5, 9), and a sinner asking God to hide his face from his sins (Psalm 51:9). A treasure is hidden "in his joy", and a talent hidden because "I was afraid" (Matthew 13:44; 25:25). Sections 10.9 and 10.11.
- **Murmuring.** The Hebrew *rāgan* is the people's complaint "in your tents" against God (Deuteronomy 1:27) and the whisperer's words that separate friends (Proverbs 16:28) (10.5).
- **Remembering.** It bows the soul down and it gives hope, in two consecutive verses (Lamentations 3:20–21; Chapter 10.3).
- **The bed.** It is the same place, but what happens there goes either way. "He plots trouble while on his bed" (Psalm 36:4). "I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night" (Psalm 63:6).
- **"Good" or "evil" in your eyes.** Joshua leaves the choice to the people's own sight: "if it is evil in your eyes to serve the Lord, choose this day" (Joshua 24:15). The king honours an old man's sight: "whatever seems good to you" (2 Samuel 19:38). In Isaiah the measure is the Lord's: "you did what was evil in my eyes" (Isaiah 65:12). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Knowing good and evil.** It is the child's knowing "how to refuse the evil and choose the good" (Isaiah 7:15). It is Barzillai's palate at eighty, with the same words: "Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not?" (2 Samuel 19:35). And it is the weighing of words in a dispute: "Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good" (Job 34:4).
- **Refusing.** The Hebrew *māʾas*, "to refuse, reject, despise", is refusing the evil (Isaiah 7:15) and refusing "the waters of Shiloah that flow gently" (8:6). Elihu uses it of refusing God's terms (Job 34:33). Job turns it on himself: "therefore I despise myself, and repent" (42:6).
- **Choosing.** The Hebrew *bāḥar*, "to choose", is the choice of a master (Joshua 24:15), of a place to live (Deuteronomy 23:16), of a way (Psalm 119:30; Isaiah 66:3), of wisdom over silver (Proverbs 16:16), and of a verdict (Job 34:4).
- **Delight.** The Hebrew *ḥāpēṣ*, "to delight in", is the soul's own delight in what it chose: "their soul delights in their abominations" (Isaiah 66:3). It is also the Lord's delight as the measure of a choice. That delight is not met when people "chose what I did not delight in" (65:12), and met in those "who choose the things that please me" (56:4). The noun *ḥēpheṣ* names his settled purpose: "he shall fulfill all my purpose" (Isaiah 44:28). It names what a man cares about, and that stops at his death: "what do they care for their houses after them" (Job 21:21).
- **Good, said of the eye.** "Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor" (Proverbs 22:9). "Bountiful" is literally "good" (10.6).
- **God's delight in a person.** It is the thanks of the rescued: "he rescued me, because he delighted in me" (Psalm 18:19). It is the mockers' taunt over a sufferer: "let him rescue him, for he delights in him!" (Psalm 22:8). The claim is the same. The sufferer does not answer the mockers; he answers God: "Yet you are he who took me from the womb" (22:9) (13.1).
- **An offering.** "For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it" (Psalm 51:16). Three verses on: "then will you delight in right sacrifices, in burnt offerings and whole burnt offerings" (51:19). It is the same offering. Between the two stands "a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (51:17) (13.1).
- **Being well pleased.** The Greek *eudokeō* is the Father's word over the Son: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:17). It is also Paul's word for weaknesses he had pleaded three times to lose: "I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities" (2 Corinthians 12:10). Between his pleading and his contentment stands the answer, "My grace is sufficient for you" (12:9) (10.1).
- **Choosing a person.** God chooses "before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him" (Ephesians 1:4). He chooses people who are "blind, yet have eyes" (Isaiah 43:8, 10), and "those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith" (James 2:5). People choose by what they can already see: "men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom" (Acts 6:3). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Holiness.** It is the purpose of being chosen: "that we should be holy and blameless before him" (Ephesians 1:4). It is also a name the chosen already carry, while the inner qualities are still to be put on: "Put on then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts" (Colossians 3:12). The verses do not say how the two fit.
- **Desire beside a choice.** The soul's desire for meat is given room away from the place God chose: "you may eat within your towns whenever you desire" (Deuteronomy 12:21). The same words for the soul's desire draw a Levite to that place: "he may come when he desires" (18:6). And the soul's delight goes with a wrong choice: "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations" (Isaiah 66:3). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Despising.** Michal "despised him in her heart" when she saw the chosen king dancing before the Lord (2 Samuel 6:16). The same verb describes the servant, "one deeply despised", before whom kings will bow (Isaiah 49:7). People despise the chosen people, judging that God has rejected them (Jeremiah 33:24). And the chosen people themselves "despised the pleasant land" (Psalm 106:24). Each verse gives its own ground: honour before people, a verdict drawn from ruin, no faith in the promise.
- **Knowing that a choice was made.** Peter's hearers know it, and a quarrel ends in silence: "you know that in the early days God made a choice among you" (Acts 15:7, 12). Paul knows it of others from what he saw: "we know … that he has chosen you, because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power" (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5). Cyrus is called for the sake of the chosen "though you do not know me" (Isaiah 45:4). The world hates the chosen "because they do not know him who sent me" (John 15:21).
- **Precious.** The Hebrew *yāqār* is wisdom weighed above *"nothing you desire"* (Proverbs 3:15), the word *"rare in those days"* (1 Samuel 3:1), a visit kept *seldom* (Proverbs 25:17), *"the moon moving in splendor"* that entices a heart (Job 31:26–27), a name *"highly esteemed"* (1 Samuel 18:30), *"the lordly price"* set on a shepherd (Zechariah 11:13), and a son *"dear"* while spoken against (Jeremiah 31:20). The Greek *timios* is faith tested by fire (1 Peter 1:7), the blood of Christ (1:19), and the jewels of Babylon (Revelation 17:4). What differs is who values, what the thing is weighed against, and whether its worth is known: man does not know wisdom's worth (Job 28:13), and Saul would not give the esteem the others gave (1 Samuel 18:29–30). (10.6 *Precious*.)

**He chooses.** The verb used of a person's choosing is also used of his:
- **a place:** "the place that the Lord your God will choose out of all your tribes to put his name and make his habitation there" (Deuteronomy 12:5)
- **people, for a purpose:** "God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe" (Acts 15:7)
- **an answer to people's choosing:** "I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them, because when I called, no one answered, when I spoke, they did not listen" (Isaiah 66:4). The verse gives the reason for his choice.

Each time, zeal and persecution stand together. In Philippians the zeal is listed among his gains, and then *"whatever gain I had, I counted as loss for the sake of Christ"* (Philippians 3:7). In Galatians what ended it was not his own correction: *"he who had set me apart before I was born, and who called me by his grace, was pleased to reveal his Son to me"* (Galatians 1:15–16). And in Acts he grants his hearers the zeal he once had. I read zeal as able to be sincere and aimed at God, and still wrong, because it runs ahead of knowing. Paul meets it with his heart's desire and prayer for them, not with contempt. Such zeal can also be stirred by a report: believers *"all zealous for the law"* had *"been told about you that you teach all the Jews who are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses"* (Acts 21:20–21).

**Doing the will of God.** The verses speak of God's will as something a person prays, knows, does, or fails to do.
- **Prayed.** "Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven" (Matthew 6:10). At Gethsemane, the second time: "My Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done" (26:42), after "The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak" (26:41). The words he taught are the words he prays.
- **Asked within.** "if we ask anything according to his will he hears us" (1 John 5:14). And: "If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you" (John 15:7). I read the two together: the asking is free where the asker's will has been shaped by his words.
- **Known by willing it.** "If anyone's will is to do God's will, he will know whether the teaching is from God" (John 7:17). The willing comes before the knowing. Paul was "appointed … to know his will" (Acts 22:14), and was asked at once, "And now why do you wait?" (22:16). "Do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is" (Ephesians 5:17).
- **Known and not done.** "you … know his will and approve what is excellent" (Romans 2:18) is said to one who boasts in God and teaches others (2:17, 19–21). "And that servant who knew his master's will but did not get ready or act according to his will, will receive a severe beating" (Luke 12:47), more than the one who did not know (12:48).
- **Said, and not done.** "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven" (Matthew 7:21). Of two sons, one said "I will not, but afterward he changed his mind and went", the other "I will, sir, but did not go". "Which of the two did the will of his father?" (21:29–31). Jesus turns the changed mind toward belief: "you did not afterward change your minds and believe him" (21:32).
- **What it is, where the verses say.** "give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you" (1 Thessalonians 5:18). "For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality" (4:3), "not in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who do not know God" (4:5). "that by doing good you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish people" (1 Peter 2:15). After confession, "do his will. Separate yourselves" (Ezra 10:11).
- **With suffering, and with endurance.** "For it is better to suffer for doing good, if that should be God's will, than for doing evil" (1 Peter 3:17), and the next verse, "For Christ also suffered" (3:18). "For you have need of endurance, so that when you have done the will of God you may receive what is promised" (Hebrews 10:36).
- **Those who do it.** "For whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother" (Matthew 12:50; Mark 3:35), said with his hand stretched toward his disciples. "if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, God listens to him" (John 9:31), said by the man who had been blind.
- **God working it in them.** "equip you with everything good that you may do his will, working in us that which is pleasing in his sight" (Hebrews 13:21). God "works in you, both to will and to work" (Philippians 2:13; 10.12). The renewed mind discerns "what is the will of God" (Romans 12:2; Chapter 14). Angels do it too (13.2).

The rising is not to life for all. "An hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment" (John 5:28–29). Daniel had been told it: "many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt" (Daniel 12:2). Paul states his hope "that there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust" (Acts 24:15).

What arises has also been **shaped from outside**.

section: Wanting that owns the one who wants
paragraph: The verses give desire the verbs of a person acting on the one who wants. It is obeyed under sin as king: *"Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions"* (Romans 6:12). It is followed: *"grumblers, malcontents, following their own sinful desires"* (Jude 16); *"scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing, following their own sinful desires. They will say, 'Where is the promise of his coming?'"* (2 Peter 3:3–4). It picks what is heard: *"having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions, and will turn away from listening to the truth and wander off into myths"* (2 Timothy 4:3–4). The itch is a want to be scratched, and the teachers are gathered to scratch it. It keeps learning from arriving: *"led astray by various passions, always learning and never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth"* (3:6–7). It deceives: *"your old self … is corrupt through deceitful desires"* (Ephesians 4:22). It baits: *"each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire"* (James 1:14). That is the fisherman's or hunter's picture, and it comes before the conceiving of 1:15. It takes captive: *"the treacherous are taken captive by their lust"* (Proverbs 11:6). It crouches like an animal at the threshold: *"sin is crouching at the door. Its desire is for you, and you must rule over it"* (Genesis 4:7). And it can be inherited: *"You are of your father the devil, and your will is to do your father's desires"* (John 8:44). I read these as one act seen from different sides: the want leads, and the one who wants follows.

**Ruling within.** Even the verses in which a person rules inside himself join the rule to another act. "Whoever is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city" (Proverbs 16:32). "Its desire is for you, and you must rule over it" (Genesis 4:7). A man "having his desire under control" (1 Corinthians 7:37). "'All things are lawful for me,' but I will not be dominated by anything" (1 Corinthians 6:12): what a man is free to do can come to rule him. Elsewhere God is asked: "Keep back your servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me!" (Psalm 19:13). Or it is grace: "sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace" (Romans 6:14), with the command two verses before, "Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body" (6:12). And one thing no one rules: "No man has power to retain the spirit, or power over the day of death" (Ecclesiastes 8:8).

"Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions. Do not present your members to sin as instruments for unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God" (Romans 6:12–13). The reason follows: "For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace" (6:14). The end of sin's rule is stated as a fact and given as a command. "Do you not know that if you present yourselves to anyone as obedient slaves, you are slaves of the one whom you obey" (6:16). I read the question of who rules within as answered by whom one presents oneself to (Chapter 11, section 7).

Paul speaks of a death the believer has already died. "How can we who died to sin still live in it?" (Romans 6:2). "Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?" (6:3). "For one who has died has been set free from sin" (6:7). "So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus" (6:11).
- **To the law:** "you also have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who has been raised from the dead, in order that we may bear fruit for God" (Romans 7:4); "through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God" (Galatians 2:19).
- **To the powers of the world:** "If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the world, why, as if you were still alive in the world, do you submit to regulations" (Colossians 2:20).
- **With him:** "If we have died with him, we will also live with him" (2 Timothy 2:11). "One has died for all, therefore all have died" (2 Corinthians 5:14).

section: On God's word, and on God
paragraph:
Delight in God's word is said beside other inner acts, and it does not take their place.
- **Beside fear.** "Blessed is the man who fears the Lord, who greatly delights in his commandments!" (Psalm 112:1). Fear and delight are said of one man in one breath (*Fear* above).
- **Beside asking to be led.** "Lead me in the path of your commandments, for I delight in it. Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to selfish gain!" (Psalm 119:35–36). He gives his delight as the reason to be led, and in the next breath asks for his heart to be inclined. I read that delighting in the way does not make a man able to steer himself on it.
- **Beside not forgetting, and love.** "I will delight in your statutes; I will not forget your word" (Psalm 119:16), "as much as in all riches" (119:14). "I find my delight in your commandments, which I love" (119:47).
- **Beside meditating.** "but his delight is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he meditates day and night" (Psalm 1:2). The "but" sets the delight against the counsel, the way and the seat of the wicked (1:1). What he delights in he turns over day and night (10.4). I read the psalm naming the man by what he delights in, more than by what he avoids.
- **Under pressure.** The delight is held where other things press on it. While "princes sit plotting against me" (Psalm 119:23): "Your testimonies are my delight; they are my counselors" (119:24). What he delights in also counsels him. In affliction: "If your law had not been my delight, I would have perished in my affliction" (119:92). He does not say the law kept him, but his delight in it, and goes on, "I will never forget your precepts, for by them you have given me life" (119:93; 10.3). In anguish: "Trouble and anguish have found me out, but your commandments are my delight" (119:143). The trouble is not taken away. The delight stands beside it.
- **Joined to doing.** "I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart" (Psalm 40:8). The delight is in doing, and the law is inward. Two verses before, it is God who has "not delighted" in sacrifice (40:6; 13.1).
- **Inward, and at war.** "For I delight in the law of God, in my inner being, but I see in my members another law waging war against the law of my mind" (Romans 7:22–23). The delight is real and it is inward, and it does not carry the members with it. The cry that follows is in Chapter 2 (7:24), and the divided service in Chapter 7 (7:25).

section: Flesh in the New Testament: one word, several values
paragraph:
The same letters say what is to be done with these desires. "Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh" (Galatians 5:16). "Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires" (5:24). "Put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires" (Romans 13:14). Peter speaks of living "for the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for human passions but for the will of God" (1 Peter 4:2). In that verse "the flesh" is simply life in the body, and the passions are what it is no longer lived for. The same desires can be used on others. False teachers "entice by sensual passions of the flesh those who are barely escaping from those who live in error" (2 Peter 2:18); they "indulge in the lust of defiling passion and despise authority" (2:10). And flesh can be an outward mark to boast in: "It is those who want to make a good showing in the flesh who would force you to be circumcised", and "they desire to have you circumcised that they may boast in your flesh" (Galatians 6:12–13).
Jude sets the same acts together: "relying on their dreams, defile the flesh, reject authority, and blaspheme the glorious ones" (Jude 8). Against them he sets the archangel, who "did not presume to pronounce a blasphemous judgment, but said, 'The Lord rebuke you'" (9; 13.2). They "blaspheme all that they do not understand" (10).

The word for "natural" is *psychikos* ("natural, of the soul"), from *psychē* ("soul"). Said of the body, it carries no blame: "it is not the spiritual that is first but the natural, and then the spiritual" (1 Corinthians 15:46). Said of a person, the same word does carry blame: "The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God" (1 Corinthians 2:14). Paul does not say what a spiritual body is made of, and I do not try to.

section: God's Spirit and the human person
paragraph:
- **Comes upon:** "the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon him" (Judges 14:6; 1 Samuel 16:13).
- **Comes, and anger follows:** "And the Spirit of God rushed upon Saul when he heard these words, and his anger was greatly kindled" (1 Samuel 11:6). At Ashkelon the Spirit rushed upon Samson, and afterwards, "In hot anger he went back to his father's house" (Judges 14:19). The same anger ends, for Saul, in mercy: "Not a man shall be put to death this day" (1 Samuel 11:13). 10.13 follows it.
- **Is grieved:** the list of bitterness, wrath and anger to be put away follows "do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God" (Ephesians 4:30–31).
- **Changes a person:** "you will … be turned into another man" (1 Samuel 10:6).
- **Instructs and leads:** "You gave your good Spirit to instruct them" (Nehemiah 9:20). "Teach me to do your will, for you are my God! Let your good Spirit lead me on level ground!" (Psalm 143:10).
- **Carries those who speak:** "no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit" (2 Peter 1:21).
- **Fills with ability:** "I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship" (Exodus 31:3).
- **Enters and sets on one's feet:** "the Spirit entered into me and set me on my feet" (Ezekiel 2:2).

**Where it comes from between people.**
- **Money.** "The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is the slave of the lender" (Proverbs 22:7). Two verses on: "Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor" (22:9).
- **A decree.** After Vashti refused the king (10.13), the counsel was that the noble women "will say the same to all the king's officials, and there will be contempt and wrath in plenty" (Esther 1:18). The decree was meant to bring it about that "all women will give honor to their husbands" (1:20), and "that every man be master in his own household" (1:22). Honour is ordered by law, out of fear of contempt.
- **Given to each other.** In marriage "the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does" (1 Corinthians 7:4). The reason follows: "so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control" (7:5). Each holds the other's authority, so that neither is left alone with what he does not rule.

**Given before it is held.**
- "You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above" (John 19:11). "For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God" (Romans 13:1).
- Even power over what a person already owns is given: "Everyone also to whom God has given wealth and possessions and power to enjoy them, and to accept his lot and rejoice in his toil — this is the gift of God" (Ecclesiastes 5:19). And it can be withheld: "yet God does not give him power to enjoy them, but a stranger enjoys them" (6:2).
- It is received from men: Saul acted "after receiving authority from the chief priests" (Acts 26:10). It follows money: "The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is the slave of the lender" (Proverbs 22:7). In marriage each holds it for the other: "the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does" (1 Corinthians 7:4).
- So the question asked of authority is where it comes from. Jesus was asked, "By what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority?" His questioners would not answer the same question about John, "we are afraid of the crowd", and said, "We do not know" (Matthew 21:23–27).

section: Care, discouragement and hiding between people
paragraph:
What one person carries inside can be for another, or done to another.
- **Care for another is a good anxiety.** Paul's "daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches" is to be weak with the weak (2 Corinthians 11:28–29). Members of one body are to "have the same care for one another" (1 Corinthians 12:25). Section 10.1 sets out the difference between this care and anxiety for oneself.
- **Losing heart is done by another.** "Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged" (Colossians 3:21). Every use of the words for losing heart has another party behind it (10.1).
- **A whisperer separates friends.** "A whisperer separates close friends" (Proverbs 16:28), and "where there is no whisperer, quarreling ceases" (26:20) (10.5).
- **People hide from people, and hide one another.** The weaker side hides: "When the wicked rise, people hide themselves" (Proverbs 28:28). Rahab and Obadiah hid others to keep them alive (Joshua 2:4; 1 Kings 18:4). And no one can hide from a friend who turns: "it is not an adversary who deals insolently with me — then I could hide from him. But it is you, a man, my equal" (Psalm 55:12–13). Section 10.11 follows all of this.

The Bible's words for anxiety do not all mean the same thing either.
- ***Merimnaō*, "to be anxious, to care".** This is the Greek word for anxiety about food and clothing (Matthew 6:25–34). It is also the word for Paul's "daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches" (2 Corinthians 11:28), for Timothy, who "will be genuinely concerned for your welfare" (Philippians 2:20), and for the members of the body who "have the same care for one another" (1 Corinthians 12:25). The word is not bad in itself. What it is about decides what it is.
- ***Meteōrizō*, "to be held in suspense".** Luke uses it once, in the same teaching: "do not seek what you are to eat and what you are to drink, nor be worried" (Luke 12:29).
- ***Dāʾag*, "to be anxious, to dread", and *deʾāgāh*, "anxiety".** The Hebrew word looks ahead to a harm that may come. The tribes east of the Jordan built their altar "from fear that in time to come your children might say to our children, 'What have you to do with the Lord, the God of Israel?'" (Joshua 22:24). Zedekiah would not surrender: "I am afraid of the Judeans who have deserted to the Chaldeans" (Jeremiah 38:19). And the "dread" of Isaiah 57:11, which led to a lie and to forgetting God (in the fear section above), is this word. Yet the psalmist turns the same word on his own sin: "I confess my iniquity; I am sorry for my sin" (Psalm 38:18).
- ***Śarʿappîm*, "anxious thoughts".** "When the cares of my heart are many, your consolations cheer my soul" (Psalm 94:19). "Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts!" (Psalm 139:23).

section: 1. The inner being is acted upon as much as it acts
paragraph:

- **God hardens.** "The Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt" (Exodus 14:8). "The Lord your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate" (Deuteronomy 2:30).
- **Dread is laid on, given, and comes upon.** "The Lord your God will lay the fear of you and the dread of you on all the land that you shall tread" (Deuteronomy 11:25). section: The heart has its own sight
paragraph: A few verses give the heart its own senses. "The eyes of your hearts enlightened" (Ephesians 1:18). God "has shone in our hearts" (2 Corinthians 4:6). "A veil lies over their hearts" (2 Corinthians 3:15). And the lover in the Song says, "I slept, but my heart was awake" (Song of Songs 5:2).

This death is spoken of as done, and a putting to death is still to be done. "Put to death therefore what is earthly in you" (Colossians 3:5); "if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live" (Romans 8:13). Paul also carries a death in his body: "always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our bodies" (2 Corinthians 4:10).

Scripture speaks of the heart being set, inclined and directed, and of the state it is in:
- **Inclined, and asked for.** *"Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to selfish gain!"* (Psalm 119:36). The one who prays this has just chosen (119:30), and asks God to do the inclining.
- **Whole or divided.** *"unite my heart to fear your name"* (Psalm 86:11), against *"a double heart"* (Psalm 12:2). Solomon's *"heart was not wholly true to the Lord his God"* (1 Kings 11:4).
- **Stubborn.** *"the stubbornness of their evil hearts"* runs through Jeremiah (Jeremiah 7:24).
- **Moved from within.** *"everyone whose heart stirred him, and everyone whose spirit moved him"* (Exodus 35:21) puts heart and spirit side by side in setting out to give.
- **Set, beside a wrong love.** Jehoshaphat was told, *"Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the Lord? Because of this, wrath has gone out against you from the Lord. Nevertheless, some good is found in you, for you destroyed the Asheroth out of the land, and have set your heart to seek God"* (2 Chronicles 19:2–3). A love wrongly given and a heart set to seek God stand in one king, and the prophet's verdict holds both.
- **Set as an aim.** The word for ambition is used three times by Paul, and its aims are not what ambition usually seeks: *"I make it my ambition to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named"* (Romans 15:20); *"whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ"* (2 Corinthians 5:9–10); *"aspire to live quietly, and to mind your own affairs, and to work with your hands"* (1 Thessalonians 4:11). Also: *"If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task"* (1 Timothy 3:1). I read the aims as going where no one has gone, pleasing him wherever one is, and quietness.

section: Life and death set before a person
paragraph:
Death is set before the inner being in the same words: *"Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death"* (Jeremiah 21:8).
- **A way can seem right and still end there.** *"There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death"* (Proverbs 14:12).
- **A choice can be made with death in view.** Esau: *"I am about to die; of what use is a birthright to me?"* (Genesis 25:32).
- **A death can set the direction of a life.** *"he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised"* (2 Corinthians 5:15).
- **A choice between two goods can stay open.** *"Yet which I shall choose I cannot tell. I am hard pressed between the two. My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better. But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account"* (Philippians 1:22–24). Paul does not settle it by choosing. He goes on: *"Convinced of this, I know that I will remain and continue with you all"* (1:25).
