- **The mortal body given life:** "he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you" (Romans 8:11). The body itself is still waited for: "we … groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies" (Romans 8:23). Chapter 2 ("The body raised") gives the account.
- **The dead in trespasses made alive:** "you, who were dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses" (Colossians 2:13). "Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life … has passed from death to life" (John 5:24).
- **Died to sin, and to the law:** "How can we who died to sin still live in it?" (Romans 6:2). "For one who has died has been set free from sin" (Romans 6:7). "For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God" (Galatians 2:19). "we are released from the law, having died to that which held us captive, so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit" (Romans 7:6). Chapter 2 ("Dead to sin") sets this death beside being dead in trespasses.
- **What is earthly put to death:** "Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry" (Colossians 3:5). "if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live" (Romans 8:13).
- **Resting on his death:** "we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son" (Romans 5:10). "he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised" (2 Corinthians 5:15). Chapter 2 ("Made alive") gives the account.
- **Turned, and living:** "For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord God; so turn, and live" (Ezekiel 18:32). Chapter 2 gives the account.
claims_sourcing_verse: C-161 (current): That death changes how the living live: no longer for themselves, dead to sin, Christ living in them

paragraph:
The verses on freely offering say more about where it comes from.
- **Asked for, then given.** "Who then will offer willingly, consecrating himself today to the Lord?" (1 Chronicles 29:5). "Then the leaders of fathers' houses made their freewill offerings" (29:6). David prays over it: "But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able thus to offer willingly? For all things come from you, and of your own have we given you" (29:14), and "all this abundance … comes from your hand and is all your own" (29:16).
- **Stirred, and helped by others.** "everyone whose spirit God had stirred to go up to rebuild", and those about them "aided them … besides all that was freely offered" (Ezra 1:5–6). Some "made freewill offerings for the house of God … according to their ability" (2:68–69).
- **Even from a foreign king.** "the silver and gold that the king and his counselors have freely offered to the God of Israel", with "the freewill offerings of the people and the priests, vowed willingly" (Ezra 7:15–16). The same decree lets "anyone … who freely offers to go to Jerusalem" go (7:13).
- **Offering oneself.** "That the leaders took the lead in Israel, that the people offered themselves willingly, bless the Lord!" (Judges 5:2). "a volunteer for the service of the Lord" (2 Chronicles 17:16). After lots were cast for who would live in Jerusalem, "the people blessed all the men who willingly offered to live in Jerusalem" (Nehemiah 11:1–2).
- **Readiness, and what it is measured by.** "a year ago started not only to do this work but also to desire to do it. So now finish doing it as well, so that your readiness in desiring it may be matched by your completing it out of what you have. For if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have" (2 Corinthians 8:10–12). The gift is carried "to show our good will" (8:19).
I read the willing offering as answered by gladness and blessing in these verses, and measured by what a person has, not by its size.

section: The heart has its own sight
paragraph: A few verses give the heart its own senses. "The eyes of your hearts enlightened" (Ephesians 1:18). God "has shone in our hearts" (2 Corinthians 4:6). "A veil lies over their hearts" (2 Corinthians 3:15). And the lover in the Song says, "I slept, but my heart was awake" (Song of Songs 5:2).

For people already chosen, Paul prays for *"the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you"* (Ephesians 1:18). Faith is shown in what it does: *"faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead"* (James 2:17).

The same passage ends a hostility between people: *"For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility"* (Ephesians 2:14), *"thereby killing the hostility. And he came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near. For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father"* (2:16–18). Those who were far and those who were near receive the same peace. I read two distances closed together: from God, and between the two peoples, with the hostility itself put to death.

section: God's Spirit and the human person
paragraph:
- **Comes upon:** "the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon him" (Judges 14:6; 1 Samuel 16:13).
- **Comes, and anger follows:** "And the Spirit of God rushed upon Saul when he heard these words, and his anger was greatly kindled" (1 Samuel 11:6). At Ashkelon the Spirit rushed upon Samson, and afterwards, "In hot anger he went back to his father's house" (Judges 14:19). The same anger ends, for Saul, in mercy: "Not a man shall be put to death this day" (1 Samuel 11:13). 10.13 follows it.
- **Is grieved:** the list of bitterness, wrath and anger to be put away follows "do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God" (Ephesians 4:30–31).
- **Changes a person:** "you will … be turned into another man" (1 Samuel 10:6).
- **Instructs and leads:** "You gave your good Spirit to instruct them" (Nehemiah 9:20). "Teach me to do your will, for you are my God! Let your good Spirit lead me on level ground!" (Psalm 143:10).
- **Carries those who speak:** "no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit" (2 Peter 1:21).
- **Fills with ability:** "I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship" (Exodus 31:3).
- **Enters and sets on one's feet:** "the Spirit entered into me and set me on my feet" (Ezekiel 2:2).
- **Is put within:** "I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes" (Ezekiel 36:27).
- **Is given into the heart:** "God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, 'Abba! Father!'" (Galatians 4:6). God "has … given us his Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee" (2 Corinthians 1:22).
- **Pours love into the heart:** "God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit" (Romans 5:5).
- **Dwells in the body:** "your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you" (1 Corinthians 6:19).
- **Bears witness beside our spirit:** "The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God" (Romans 8:16).
- **Strengthens the inner being:** Ephesians 3:16.
- **Intercedes:** "the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words" (Romans 8:26).

section: Wanting that owns the one who wants
paragraph: What the verses set against it is not a stronger want either. In two places the uncontrolled desire stands beside not knowing God: *"not in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who do not know God"* (1 Thessalonians 4:5); *"do not be conformed to the passions of your former ignorance"* (1 Peter 1:14). Against deceitful desires stands a mind made new: *"to be renewed in the spirit of your minds, and to put on the new self"* (Ephesians 4:23–24). Against passions that pass stands the will of God, which lasts: *"so as to live for the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for human passions but for the will of God. For the time that is past suffices for doing what the Gentiles want to do"* (1 Peter 4:2–3); *"the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life … the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever"* (1 John 2:16–17). And there is a share in his nature: *"partakers of the divine nature, having escaped from the corruption that is in the world because of sinful desire"* (2 Peter 1:4).

The verses also name the way out. "Truly, truly, I say to you, an hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live" (John 5:25); "whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me … has passed from death to life" (5:24). God "made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses" (Colossians 2:13). To believers: "Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you" (Ephesians 5:14). The lost son "came to himself" and went home, and his father calls it coming alive (Luke 15:17–24). John gives a sign that it has happened: "We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers" (1 John 3:14). "Made alive", below, follows this.
claims_sourcing_verse: C-148 (current): The verses name the way out of death in the living: hearing the Son and believing, God making alive with forgiveness, waking, coming home; loving the brothers is its sign

paragraph:
Death, too, can belong to the Lord. Paul says it plainly: "For none of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself. For if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord's" (Romans 14:7–8). "For to this end Christ died and lived again, that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living" (14:9). He says it of himself: "Christ will be honored in my body, whether by life or by death. For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain" (Philippians 1:20–21). And to a church: "whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future—all are yours" (1 Corinthians 3:22). And he speaks of a dying that goes on while he lives:
- "I die every day!" (1 Corinthians 15:31)
- "For we who live are always being given over to death for Jesus' sake, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our mortal flesh" (2 Corinthians 4:11)
- "as dying, and behold, we live" (2 Corinthians 6:9)
- "So death is at work in us, but life in you" (2 Corinthians 4:12)
claims_sourcing_verse: C-162 (current): A death, too, can belong to the Lord, and a dying can go on while a person lives

paragraph:
- **The lowly spirit and the contrite heart revived:** "I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly, and to revive the heart of the contrite" (Isaiah 57:15). God's reason is tender: "I will not contend forever … for the spirit would grow faint before me" (57:16).
- **The soul restored:** "He restores my soul" (Psalm 23:3). "The law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul" (Psalm 19:7). "Receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls" (James 1:21). "Having purified your souls by your obedience to the truth" (1 Peter 1:22).
- **The conscience cleansed:** "the blood of Christ … [will] purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God" (Hebrews 9:14). "Let us draw near with a true heart … with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience" (Hebrews 10:22).
- **The mind renewed:** "be renewed in the spirit of your minds" (Ephesians 4:23). "Be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God" (Romans 12:2).
- **The inner self renewed daily:** "Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day" (2 Corinthians 4:16).
- **The whole person transformed:** "We all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit" (2 Corinthians 3:18).
- **The straying spirit and the murmuring mouth taught:** "those who go astray in spirit will come to understanding, and those who murmur will accept instruction" (Isaiah 29:24).
- **The life kept hidden:** "For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God" (Colossians 3:3).
- **Born again to a living hope:** God "has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead" (1 Peter 1:3). Paul: "that I may know him and the power of his resurrection" (Philippians 3:10).
- **The mortal body given life:** "he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you" (Romans 8:11). The body itself is still waited for: "we … groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies" (Romans 8:23). Chapter 2 ("The body raised") gives the account.
- **The dead in trespasses made alive:** "you, who were dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses" (Colossians 2:13). "Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life … has passed from death to life" (John 5:24).
- **Died to sin, and to the law:** "How can we who died to sin still live in it?" (Romans 6:2). "For one who has died has been set free from sin" (Romans 6:7). "For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God" (Galatians 2:19). "we are released from the law, having died to that which held us captive, so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit" (Romans 7:6). Chapter 2 ("Dead to sin") sets this death beside being dead in trespasses.
- **What is earthly put to death:** "Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry" (Colossians 3:5). "if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live" (Romans 8:13).
- **Resting on his death:** "we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son" (Romans 5:10). "he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised" (2 Corinthians 5:15). Chapter 2 ("Made alive") gives the account.
- **Turned, and living:** "For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord God; so turn, and live" (Ezekiel 18:32). Chapter 2 gives the account.

The change is to be like him. "Our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body, by the power that enables him even to subject all things to himself" (Philippians 3:20–21). John says how much is still hidden: "what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is" (1 John 3:2).

"But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20). "For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive. But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ" (15:22–23). He is "the firstborn from the dead" (Colossians 1:18). "God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power" (1 Corinthians 6:14). Peter says death could not keep him: "God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it" (Acts 2:24). He and Paul read the psalm of him: "For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, or let your Holy One see corruption" (Acts 2:27). "For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption, but he whom God raised up did not see corruption" (Acts 13:36–37).

- **Return begins with thoughts.** "Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts; let him return to the Lord, that he may have compassion on him" (Isaiah 55:7).
- **A hostile mind is reconciled.** "And you, who once were alienated and hostile in mind, doing evil deeds, he has now reconciled in his body of flesh by his death" (Colossians 1:21–22).
- **Thoughts are taken captive.** "We destroy arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God, and take every thought captive to obey Christ" (2 Corinthians 10:5).
- **The mind is renewed.** "Be transformed by the renewal of your mind" (Romans 12:2).
- **I am told to reckon as God reckons.** "Consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus" (Romans 6:11). The word is the reckoning word: I am to count myself as God counts me.
- **Thinking is directed.** "Whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable … think about these things" (Philippians 4:8).
- **The leaning is kept.** David has seen his people "offering freely and joyously to you" (1 Chronicles 29:17), and he prays: "keep forever such purposes and thoughts in the hearts of your people, and direct their hearts toward you" (29:18). The purposes are that free and joyful giving. "You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you" (Isaiah 26:3).
- **The mind is made ready.** "Preparing your minds for action, and being sober-minded, set your hope fully on the grace that will be brought to you" (1 Peter 1:13).
- **Thinking grows up.** "When I became a man, I gave up childish ways" (1 Corinthians 13:11).

**The Father's will, said of creation and of people.** "for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created" (Revelation 4:11). "God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose" (1 Corinthians 12:18). "God chose to make known how great among the Gentiles are the riches of the glory of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory" (Colossians 1:27). Christ "gave himself for our sins … according to the will of our God and Father" (Galatians 1:4). God "desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth" (1 Timothy 2:4). And after the shepherd who rejoices over the one found: "So it is not the will of my Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish" (Matthew 18:14).

And Scripture names life itself as a person. Moses says of the Lord, "he is your life and length of days" (Deuteronomy 30:20). Paul speaks of "Christ who is your life" (Colossians 3:4). At Lazarus's grave Jesus says it of himself: "I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live" (John 11:25). Jesus says where his own life comes from, and where his people's comes from: "For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself" (John 5:26); "Because I live, you also will live" (John 14:19). And he says what life is: "this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent" (John 17:3).

Anger touches many of the activities in this Part. The verses join it to the others in their own wording: by "so", "therefore" and "lest", by "but", by naming them together, and by sharing a root.
- **Fear** (10.12): Moses afraid of the anger, and heard (Deuteronomy 9:19); afraid, then enraged (Daniel 11:30); angry, then afraid (2 Samuel 6:8–9); not afraid of the king's anger (Hebrews 11:27). The two share a root in *rāgaz*, "to tremble", rendered "Be angry" (Psalm 4:4). "Who considers the power of your anger, and your wrath according to the fear of you?" (Psalm 90:11).
- **Feeling** (10.1): anger beside grief. Jonathan "was grieved for David" (1 Samuel 20:34). Jesus was angry and grieved at once (Mark 3:5). "Godly grief produces a repentance", and with it indignation (2 Corinthians 7:10–11).
- **Knowing and hearing** (10.2): anger is kindled on hearing, and God's anger is said to end in knowing (Ezekiel 5:13) and to be understood later (Jeremiah 23:20).
- **Remembering** (10.3): "Remember and do not forget how you provoked the Lord your God to wrath" (Deuteronomy 9:7). When the king's anger abated, "he remembered Vashti" (Esther 2:1).
- **Speaking** (10.5): "A soft answer turns away wrath" (Proverbs 15:1); rash words from an embittered spirit (Psalm 106:33); "slow to speak, slow to anger" (James 1:19).
- **Wanting** (10.6): jealousy with anger (Proverbs 6:34); "You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel" (James 4:2).
- **Relating to God** (10.9): God's anger, provoked, pleaded against, borne and turned.
- **Relating to others** (10.10): the ruler's anger; strife between people; turning another's anger away.
- **Going wrong** (Chapter 12): the lists of what is put away; "one given to anger causes much transgression" (Proverbs 29:22).
- **Made new** (Chapter 14): putting off anger with the old self (Colossians 3:8–10); delivered from the wrath to come.
- **Life and death** (Chapter 2): "the wrath of God remains on him" (John 3:36); "A king's wrath is a messenger of death" (Proverbs 16:14).
- **The heart and the spirit** (Chapters 4 and 6): anger burns within, lodges in the heart of fools, and comes in the heat of the spirit.

**What the chosen are called to.** Being chosen is given as the ground of commands:
- **Be strong and do it.** *"the Lord has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary; be strong and do it"* (1 Chronicles 28:10), with *"serve him with a whole heart and with a willing mind, for the Lord searches all hearts"* (28:9).
- **Put on.** *"Put on then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience"* (Colossians 3:12). What is put on is turned toward others: *"as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive"* (3:13); *"above all these put on love"* (3:14).
- **Stand firm.** *"stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught by us"* (2 Thessalonians 2:15).
- **Confirm it.** *"be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election, for if you practice these qualities you will never fall"* (2 Peter 1:10). The qualities are added one to another, from faith to love (1:5–7). The effort follows what was given first: *"His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness"* (1:3).
- **Remember.** *"Remember the wondrous works that he has done … children of Jacob, his chosen ones!"* (Psalm 105:5–6); *"Remember these things, O Jacob … you will not be forgotten by me"* (Isaiah 44:21).

The same words change face with the setting, and the verses show why.
- **"Good" or "evil" in your eyes.**
  - It is the chooser's own sight, where turning from the Lord could begin (Joshua 24:15).
  - It is the chooser's own good, honoured by the king (2 Samuel 19:38).
  - It gives way to *"evil in my eyes"*, the Lord's sight (Isaiah 65:12).
  - *Why:* in Joshua and Isaiah the choice is between the Lord and other gods. With Barzillai it is where an old man who served will live.
- **Knowing good and evil.**
  - It is the knowing that stands under the choice of right and wrong (Isaiah 7:15–16).
  - It is the palate's knowing of the pleasant and the unpleasant, which fades at eighty (2 Samuel 19:35).
  - It is the weighing of words in a dispute (Job 34:3–4).
  - *Why:* the same knowing is turned to right and wrong, to taste, and to judgement.
- **Refusing.**
  - It is refusing the evil (Isaiah 7:15) and refusing the gentle waters (8:6).
  - It is refusing God's terms, as Elihu charges (Job 34:33).
  - It is Job turning it on himself in repentance (42:6).
  - *Why:* the act is the same; what it is aimed at decides whether it is right.
- **Choosing.** It is the choice of a master (Joshua 24:15), a place (Deuteronomy 23:16), a way (Psalm 119:30; Isaiah 66:3), a preference (Proverbs 16:16) and a verdict (Job 34:4). *Why:* it is turned to whatever is set before a person.
- **Delight.** It is the soul's own delight in what it chose (Isaiah 66:3), and it is the Lord's delight as the measure, either not met (65:12; 66:4) or met (56:4). *Why:* whose delight it is decides.
- **Choosing a person.**
  - God chooses before anything in the person, *"before the foundation of the world"* (Ephesians 1:4). He chooses people who are blind and deaf (Isaiah 43:8, 10), and the poor (James 2:5).
  - People choose by what is already seen: *"men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom"* (Acts 6:3).
  - *Why:* who chooses. With God, the inner life is what the choosing is for. With people, it is the measure.
- **Holiness.**
  - It is the purpose of the choosing: *"that we should be holy and blameless before him"* (Ephesians 1:4).
  - It is a name the chosen already carry, while the inner qualities are still to be put on: *"as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved"* (Colossians 3:12).
  - *Why:* the verses do not say. I set them side by side.
- **Desire beside a choice.**
  - The soul's desire for meat is given room away from the place God chose (Deuteronomy 12:21).
  - The same desire of the soul draws a Levite to that place (18:6).
  - The soul delights in its own abominations, beside a wrong choice (Isaiah 66:3).
  - *Why:* what the desire is turned toward. The first two are allowed in the same words. In the third it is what the soul delights in that decides.
- **Despising.**
  - Others despise the one chosen: Michal *"in her heart"*, by the eyes of people (2 Samuel 6:16, 20); the servant *"deeply despised"*, with kings to bow before him (Isaiah 49:7). It is the same verb in both.
  - People despise the chosen people, concluding God rejected them (Jeremiah 33:24).
  - The chosen people themselves *"despised the pleasant land"* (Psalm 106:24).
  - *Why:* who despises what. Each verse gives its own ground: honour before people, a verdict drawn from ruin, no faith in the promise.

- **A tender heart.** It melts before an enemy and spreads fear to others (Deuteronomy 20:8). But Josiah's heart "was penitent [tender]" before God's word, and God answered him with peace (2 Kings 22:19–20). The same softness is cowardice in one place and repentance in the other.
- **A strong heart.** "Be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the Lord!" (Psalm 27:14). With Absalom, the same verb gives his servants the nerve to kill: "be courageous and be valiant" (2 Samuel 13:28). With Pharaoh it is hardening: "I will harden his heart" (Exodus 4:21), literally *strengthen*.
- **A guarded heart.** "Keep your heart with all vigilance" (Proverbs 4:23). Three chapters later the same word describes the adulteress, "wily [guarded] of heart" (Proverbs 7:10).
- **Crushing.** Crushed by an enemy, the spirit collapses (Psalm 143:3–4). Offered to God, a crushed spirit is the very sacrifice he wants: "a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (Psalm 51:17).
- **Loving and hating one's own soul** (Chapter 5).
- **Devising.** The same Hebrew verb describes the craftsmen who worked cherubim "skillfully" into the tabernacle curtains (Exodus 26:1) and those who plot. One word for planning means "discretion" (Proverbs 2:11), "evil devices" (Proverbs 12:2), and God's own purpose: "no purpose of yours can be thwarted" (Job 42:2).
- **Planning against.** God says, "I am … devising a plan against you. Return" (Jeremiah 18:11), and the people say, "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah" (18:18). The word and the "against" are the same. One plan is meant to bring people back, and the other is meant to silence the one who calls them.
- **Purposing.** The verb for purposing (*zāmam*) is the psalmist's resolve: "I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress" (Psalm 17:3). It is the wicked man's plot: "The wicked plots against the righteous" (Psalm 37:12). It is the wise woman's weighing: "She considers a field and buys it" (Proverbs 31:16). And it is God's fixed purpose: "I have purposed; I have not relented" (Jeremiah 4:28). I read the change as following whom it is aimed at: one's own mouth, another's harm, one's own household, or a whole land.
- **Willing.** The Hebrew word for being willing (*ʾāḇâ*) is almost always a "no". It is the guard's refusal to kill the priests (1 Samuel 22:17), David refusing the water for the men's sake (2 Samuel 23:17), Amnon refusing Tamar's plea (2 Samuel 13:14), and Israel refusing God's rest (Isaiah 30:15). God himself is "not willing to destroy" (2 Kings 8:19), and "will not be willing to forgive" the man who blesses himself in his stubbornness (Deuteronomy 29:20). The Greek word runs from Pilate "wishing to satisfy the crowd" (Mark 15:15) to God "not wishing that any should perish" (2 Peter 3:9). Each passage gives the reason: faith, honour, force, fear, grief, covenant, love, a self-blessing heart. I read the change as following what is refused, and for whose sake (10.7, *Willing*).
- **Planning ahead.** The same looking ahead is a king's honest count of his strength (Luke 14:31) and sailors' guess "on the chance that somehow" (Acts 27:12). It is a man's "aim in life" (2 Timothy 3:10) and a plot "to put him to death" (John 11:53). I read the verses as setting the difference beside how much the planner can see. The king can count, the sailors cannot see the reef, and over all of it "the Lord establishes his steps" (Proverbs 16:9).
- **Reckoning.** People misreckon: "we esteemed him stricken" (Isaiah 53:4). God reckons faith "as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6). The law reckons in order to release (Leviticus 25:50). Love refuses to reckon at all: it "is not … resentful" (1 Corinthians 13:5).
- **Likening.** Comparing is how love praises ("I compare you, my love", Song of Songs 1:9), how comfort reaches out (Lamentations 2:13), and how worship ends ("who in the skies can be compared to the Lord?", Psalm 89:6). It is also how pride rises: "I will make myself like the Most High" (Isaiah 14:14).
- **Reasoning.** The Greek word is Mary's honest pondering (Luke 1:29), the disciples' anxious circling (Mark 8:17), and a quarrel (Philippians 2:14; 1 Timothy 2:8).
- **The nose.** The Hebrew word for anger, *ʾaph*, is the nostril where God breathed in life (Genesis 2:7), the face bowed in worship (2 Chronicles 7:3), and the face lifted in pride (Psalm 10:4). It can be given a ring in love (Ezekiel 16:12) or a hook for raging (2 Kings 19:28). "Long of nostrils" is patience, in God and in the wise (Exodus 34:6; Proverbs 14:29).
- **Anger.** Jesus's anger heals (Mark 3:5). A crowd's anger stops its ears and kills (Acts 7:57–58). "Be angry and do not sin" (Ephesians 4:26).
- **Vexation.** It is provocation done to another (1 Samuel 1:6), suffering borne (1:16), and "Sorrow is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad" (Ecclesiastes 7:3).
- **Provoking.** Love "is not irritable" (1 Corinthians 13:5), with the same word that tells believers to "stir up one another to love and good works" (Hebrews 10:24).
- **Overflow.** One Hebrew word, *ʿebrah*, is the overflow of anger and the overflow of pride. God offers it to Job with irony: "Pour out the overflowings of your anger, and look on everyone who is proud and abase him" (Job 40:11). And "'Scoffer' is the name of the arrogant, haughty man who acts with arrogant pride" (Proverbs 21:24), where the word is the same.
- **Storm.** The same storm word, *sāʿar*, is the angry king's mind ("the mind of the king of Syria was greatly troubled", 2 Kings 6:11) and the suffering city ("O afflicted one, storm-tossed and not comforted", Isaiah 54:11).
- **Denouncing.** "How can I curse whom God has not cursed?" (Numbers 23:8). But "Whoever says to the wicked, 'You are in the right,' will be cursed by peoples, abhorred by nations" (Proverbs 24:24). The word is empty when it goes against God's verdict, and it lands when it follows justice.
- **A creed.** "Slow to anger" is used in worship, in pleading, in confession, in Jonah's complaint, in praise, in wonder, in announcing judgment, and as the ground for returning (Chapter 10.9).
- **Mourning.** Aaron is forbidden to mourn "lest … wrath come" (Leviticus 10:6). When the wrath has come, mourning is commanded (Jeremiah 4:8).
- **God's hand.** The "mighty hand" brought Israel out (Deuteronomy 6:21) and later fought "against you … in anger" (Jeremiah 21:5).
- **Fear.** One word, *yārēʾ*, "to fear", names the fear that drives a person away from God and the fear of God that keeps a person from sin. In one sentence Moses takes the first away and sets the second in its place: "Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin" (Exodus 20:20). The same people, with the same word, are afraid of Egypt and then fear the Lord (Exodus 14:10, 31). Turned round, the word describes the one who is feared: "the great and awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love" (Nehemiah 1:5). Beside a choice it has three more faces. It is learned at a feast in the place God chose: "that you may learn to fear the Lord your God always" (Deuteronomy 14:23). It falls on those who hear of presumption punished: "all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again" (17:13). And it comes as terror on people who resisted God's choice once he made it plain: "Are we all to perish?" (Numbers 17:13). Section 10.1 sets out the word, and 10.7 the faces beside a choice.
- **"Do not fear."** God says it with a reason, and the reason is himself: "for I am with you" (Isaiah 41:10). Joseph says it and refuses to stand in God's place (Genesis 50:19, 21). Jael says it before the tent peg (Judges 4:18). The words are the same. What they are for is not.
- **Trembling and dread.** The Hebrew words for trembling and dread are rendered as fear, and also as "Be angry" (Psalm 4:4), "deeply moved" (2 Samuel 18:33), a heart that "trembled for the ark of God" (1 Samuel 4:13), and "your heart shall thrill and exult" (Isaiah 60:5). I read them as naming one inner stirring, which its situation turns into fear, anger, grief, care or joy (10.1).
- **"None shall make you afraid."** It is promised peace: "I will give peace in the land, and you shall lie down, and none shall make you afraid" (Leviticus 26:6). The same Hebrew phrase is used of desolation: "The cities of Aroer are deserted; they will be for flocks, which will lie down, and none will make them afraid" (Isaiah 17:2). One phrase describes rest for a people and the emptiness left when they are gone.
- **Care.** The Greek *merimnaō*, "to be anxious, to care", is rebuked when it is about my own food and clothing (Matthew 6:25) and praised when it is "genuinely concerned for your welfare" (Philippians 2:20). The Hebrew *dāʾag*, "to be anxious, to dread", is dread of what may come (Jeremiah 38:19), a father's worry for his son (1 Samuel 10:2), and sorrow for sin: "I am sorry for my sin" (Psalm 38:18). Section 10.1 sets this out.
- **Hiding.** The Hebrew *sātar*, "to hide", is God hiding a person in safety and God hiding his face, four verses apart (Psalm 27:5, 9), and a sinner asking God to hide his face from his sins (Psalm 51:9). A treasure is hidden "in his joy", and a talent hidden because "I was afraid" (Matthew 13:44; 25:25). Sections 10.9 and 10.11.
- **Murmuring.** The Hebrew *rāgan* is the people's complaint "in your tents" against God (Deuteronomy 1:27) and the whisperer's words that separate friends (Proverbs 16:28) (10.5).
- **Remembering.** It bows the soul down and it gives hope, in two consecutive verses (Lamentations 3:20–21; Chapter 10.3).
- **The bed.** It is the same place, but what happens there goes either way. "He plots trouble while on his bed" (Psalm 36:4). "I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night" (Psalm 63:6).
- **"Good" or "evil" in your eyes.** Joshua leaves the choice to the people's own sight: "if it is evil in your eyes to serve the Lord, choose this day" (Joshua 24:15). The king honours an old man's sight: "whatever seems good to you" (2 Samuel 19:38). In Isaiah the measure is the Lord's: "you did what was evil in my eyes" (Isaiah 65:12). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Knowing good and evil.** It is the child's knowing "how to refuse the evil and choose the good" (Isaiah 7:15). It is Barzillai's palate at eighty, with the same words: "Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not?" (2 Samuel 19:35). And it is the weighing of words in a dispute: "Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good" (Job 34:4).
- **Refusing.** The Hebrew *māʾas*, "to refuse, reject, despise", is refusing the evil (Isaiah 7:15) and refusing "the waters of Shiloah that flow gently" (8:6). Elihu uses it of refusing God's terms (Job 34:33). Job turns it on himself: "therefore I despise myself, and repent" (42:6).
- **Choosing.** The Hebrew *bāḥar*, "to choose", is the choice of a master (Joshua 24:15), of a place to live (Deuteronomy 23:16), of a way (Psalm 119:30; Isaiah 66:3), of wisdom over silver (Proverbs 16:16), and of a verdict (Job 34:4).
- **Delight.** The Hebrew *ḥāpēṣ*, "to delight in", is the soul's own delight in what it chose: "their soul delights in their abominations" (Isaiah 66:3). It is also the Lord's delight as the measure of a choice. That delight is not met when people "chose what I did not delight in" (65:12), and met in those "who choose the things that please me" (56:4). The noun *ḥēpheṣ* names his settled purpose: "he shall fulfill all my purpose" (Isaiah 44:28). It names what a man cares about, and that stops at his death: "what do they care for their houses after them" (Job 21:21).
- **Good, said of the eye.** "Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor" (Proverbs 22:9). "Bountiful" is literally "good" (10.6).
- **God's delight in a person.** It is the thanks of the rescued: "he rescued me, because he delighted in me" (Psalm 18:19). It is the mockers' taunt over a sufferer: "let him rescue him, for he delights in him!" (Psalm 22:8). The claim is the same. The sufferer does not answer the mockers; he answers God: "Yet you are he who took me from the womb" (22:9) (13.1).
- **An offering.** "For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it" (Psalm 51:16). Three verses on: "then will you delight in right sacrifices, in burnt offerings and whole burnt offerings" (51:19). It is the same offering. Between the two stands "a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (51:17) (13.1).
- **Being well pleased.** The Greek *eudokeō* is the Father's word over the Son: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:17). It is also Paul's word for weaknesses he had pleaded three times to lose: "I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities" (2 Corinthians 12:10). Between his pleading and his contentment stands the answer, "My grace is sufficient for you" (12:9) (10.1).
- **Choosing a person.** God chooses "before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him" (Ephesians 1:4). He chooses people who are "blind, yet have eyes" (Isaiah 43:8, 10), and "those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith" (James 2:5). People choose by what they can already see: "men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom" (Acts 6:3). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Holiness.** It is the purpose of being chosen: "that we should be holy and blameless before him" (Ephesians 1:4). It is also a name the chosen already carry, while the inner qualities are still to be put on: "Put on then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts" (Colossians 3:12). The verses do not say how the two fit.
- **Desire beside a choice.** The soul's desire for meat is given room away from the place God chose: "you may eat within your towns whenever you desire" (Deuteronomy 12:21). The same words for the soul's desire draw a Levite to that place: "he may come when he desires" (18:6). And the soul's delight goes with a wrong choice: "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations" (Isaiah 66:3). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Despising.** Michal "despised him in her heart" when she saw the chosen king dancing before the Lord (2 Samuel 6:16). The same verb describes the servant, "one deeply despised", before whom kings will bow (Isaiah 49:7). People despise the chosen people, judging that God has rejected them (Jeremiah 33:24). And the chosen people themselves "despised the pleasant land" (Psalm 106:24). Each verse gives its own ground: honour before people, a verdict drawn from ruin, no faith in the promise.
- **Knowing that a choice was made.** Peter's hearers know it, and a quarrel ends in silence: "you know that in the early days God made a choice among you" (Acts 15:7, 12). Paul knows it of others from what he saw: "we know … that he has chosen you, because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power" (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5). Cyrus is called for the sake of the chosen "though you do not know me" (Isaiah 45:4). The world hates the chosen "because they do not know him who sent me" (John 15:21).
- **Precious.** The Hebrew *yāqār* is wisdom weighed above *"nothing you desire"* (Proverbs 3:15), the word *"rare in those days"* (1 Samuel 3:1), a visit kept *seldom* (Proverbs 25:17), *"the moon moving in splendor"* that entices a heart (Job 31:26–27), a name *"highly esteemed"* (1 Samuel 18:30), *"the lordly price"* set on a shepherd (Zechariah 11:13), and a son *"dear"* while spoken against (Jeremiah 31:20). The Greek *timios* is faith tested by fire (1 Peter 1:7), the blood of Christ (1:19), and the jewels of Babylon (Revelation 17:4). What differs is who values, what the thing is weighed against, and whether its worth is known: man does not know wisdom's worth (Job 28:13), and Saul would not give the esteem the others gave (1 Samuel 18:29–30). (10.6 *Precious*.)

- **Ruling:** "he who rules his spirit [is better] than he who takes a city" (Proverbs 16:32). "Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts" (Colossians 3:15).
- **Guarding:** "Keep your heart with all vigilance" (Proverbs 4:23). "Keep your soul diligently, lest you forget" (Deuteronomy 4:9). "Guard yourselves in your spirit" (Malachi 2:15).
- **Serving:** "I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin" (Romans 7:25).
- **Judging:** "whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart" (1 John 3:20).

section: Delivered from the wrath to come
paragraph: What they do with this knowledge is not fear. They wait "for his Son from heaven … Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come" (1 Thessalonians 1:10). They "encourage one another and build one another up" (5:11).

Gathered together, the verses show a person responding to God's anger in these ways. Each is stated by its own verses.
- **Pleading:** "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak" (Genesis 18:30).
- **Humbling oneself:** "when he humbled himself the wrath of the Lord turned from him" (2 Chronicles 12:12).
- **Acting to remove the cause:** Hezekiah's covenant (2 Chronicles 29:10).
- **Reading the ruin:** "Why has the Lord done thus to this land? What caused the heat of this great anger?" (Deuteronomy 29:24).
- **Crying out from distress:** "when the people of Israel cried out to the Lord, the Lord raised up a deliverer" (Judges 3:9).
- **Refusing the warning,** "until there was no remedy" (2 Chronicles 36:16).
- **Asking for correction without the anger:** "Correct me, O Lord, but in justice; not in your anger" (Jeremiah 10:24).
- **Fearing being cast off:** "Turn not your servant away in anger" (Psalm 27:9).
- **Asking how long:** "How long, O Lord? Will you be angry forever?" (Psalm 79:5).
- **Standing in awe:** "Who can stand before you when once your anger is roused?" (Psalm 76:7).
- **Taking it into the whole of life:** "For all our days pass away under your wrath" (Psalm 90:9), and the prayer, "So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom" (90:12).
- **Sheltering while it passes:** "hide yourselves for a little while until the fury has passed by" (Isaiah 26:20).
- **Holding a false peace:** "surely his anger has turned from me" (Jeremiah 2:35).
- **Mourning:** "For this put on sackcloth, lament and wail" (Jeremiah 4:8).
- **Not taking it in:** "it burned him up, but he did not take it to heart" (Isaiah 42:25).
- **Coming to know:** "And they shall know that I am the Lord" (Ezekiel 5:13).
- **Returning without a guarantee:** "Who knows?" (Jonah 3:9).
- **Bearing it because of one's sin:** "I will bear the indignation of the Lord because I have sinned against him, until he pleads my cause" (Micah 7:9).
- **Leaving vengeance to God:** "never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God" (Romans 12:19), and then, "if your enemy is hungry, feed him" (12:20).
- **Putting off what the wrath comes on:** "But now you must put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth" (Colossians 3:8), two verses after "On account of these the wrath of God is coming" (3:6).
- **Singing that it is just:** "Just and true are your ways" (Revelation 15:3).
- **Speaking of it as a wrath one is delivered from:** "Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come" (1 Thessalonians 1:10).

Paul uses the same word of those who die believing, and he uses it to speak to grief. "But we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope." "God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep" (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14). The living "will not precede those who have fallen asleep" (4:15). Of the five hundred who saw the risen Christ, "most of whom are still alive, though some have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:6). He does not forbid the grief. He sets it apart from grief that has no hope. The hope rests on a rising: "Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20). Without that, "those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished" (15:18).

paragraph: Death is named as an enemy to be undone. "The last enemy to be destroyed is death" (1 Corinthians 15:26). The risen Christ says, "I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades" (Revelation 1:18). Paul says he "abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel" (2 Timothy 1:10).

**With the chosen, and for them.** Others stand with the chosen too. The psalmist asks to be let in: *"Remember me, O Lord, … that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation"* (Psalm 106:4–5). He asks God, not the chosen, and he asks it confessing his sin (106:6). Paul writes in chains: *"I endure everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain the salvation"* (2 Timothy 2:10). The elder loves the elect lady *"in truth"*, *"because of the truth that abides in us"* (2 John 1–2): the love rests on the truth, not on her being chosen. And whoever believes in the stone God chose *"will not be put to shame"* (1 Peter 2:6). For those who do not believe, the same stone is *"a stone of stumbling"* (2:8).

The making alive rests on a death:
- "Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:3)
- "while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8)
- "so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone" (Hebrews 2:9)
- God himself calls for it: "Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, against the man who stands next to me … Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered" (Zechariah 13:7). Jesus reads it of his own death on the night of his arrest (Matthew 26:31).
- Isaiah says it of the soul: "he poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many" (Isaiah 53:12)

paragraph: Hebrews reads Psalm 40 as the words of Christ: "Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body have you prepared for me; in burnt offerings and sin offerings you have taken no pleasure. Then I said, 'Behold, I have come to do your will, O God'" (Hebrews 10:5–7). It draws the end: "And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all" (10:10). What he had no pleasure in is set aside for a will done in a body.

**What he desires.** The verses also give his desire for a place, a people and a time:
- A place: *"For the Lord has chosen Zion; he has desired it for his dwelling place: 'This is my resting place forever; here I will dwell, for I have desired it'"* (Psalm 132:13–14). The other mountains are pictured looking on with envy: *"Why do you look with hatred, O many-peaked mountain, at the mount that God desired for his abode?"* (Psalm 68:16).
- His people, as his hope for them: *"I said, How I would set you among my sons, and give you a pleasant land, a heritage most beautiful of all nations. And I thought you would call me, My Father, and would not turn from following me. Surely, as a treacherous wife leaves her husband, so have you been treacherous to me"* (Jeremiah 3:19–20). His hope is spoken, and then its disappointment.
- His grief over what is his: *"they have made my pleasant portion a desolate wilderness. They have made it a desolation; desolate, it mourns to me. The whole land is made desolate, but no man lays it to heart"* (Jeremiah 12:10–11).
- His keeping of it: *"A pleasant vineyard, sing of it! I, the Lord, am its keeper; every moment I water it … I have no wrath"* (Isaiah 27:2–4).
- His word on the one who clings to him: *"Because he holds fast to me in love, I will deliver him; I will protect him, because he knows my name"* (Psalm 91:14).
- His guarding of what is left behind for worship: *"no one shall covet your land, when you go up to appear before the Lord your God three times in the year"* (Exodus 34:24).
- What comes to his house: *"the treasures of all nations shall come in, and I will fill this house with glory … The silver is mine, and the gold is mine"* (Haggai 2:7–8).
- His timing: *"When I please, I will discipline them"* (Hosea 10:10).
- The Son's desire: *"I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer"* (Luke 22:15).
- Job hopes for God's longing: *"You would call, and I would answer you; you would long for the work of your hands"* (Job 14:15).

section: The Old Testament does this with the heart
paragraph: The New Testament joins the two words. John speaks of the heart doing the work of conscience: "whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything. Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God" (1 John 3:20–21). In Hebrews, "hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience" (Hebrews 10:22).

- **The lowly spirit and the contrite heart revived:** "I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly, and to revive the heart of the contrite" (Isaiah 57:15). God's reason is tender: "I will not contend forever … for the spirit would grow faint before me" (57:16).
- **The soul restored:** "He restores my soul" (Psalm 23:3). "The law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul" (Psalm 19:7). "Receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls" (James 1:21). "Having purified your souls by your obedience to the truth" (1 Peter 1:22).
- **The conscience cleansed:** "the blood of Christ … [will] purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God" (Hebrews 9:14). "Let us draw near with a true heart … with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience" (Hebrews 10:22).
- **The mind renewed:** "be renewed in the spirit of your minds" (Ephesians 4:23). "Be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God" (Romans 12:2).
- **The inner self renewed daily:** "Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day" (2 Corinthians 4:16).
- **The whole person transformed:** "We all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit" (2 Corinthians 3:18).
- **The straying spirit and the murmuring mouth taught:** "those who go astray in spirit will come to understanding, and those who murmur will accept instruction" (Isaiah 29:24).
- **The life kept hidden:** "For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God" (Colossians 3:3).
- **Born again to a living hope:** God "has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead" (1 Peter 1:3). Paul: "that I may know him and the power of his resurrection" (Philippians 3:10).
- **The mortal body given life:** "he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you" (Romans 8:11). The body itself is still waited for: "we … groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies" (Romans 8:23). Chapter 2 ("The body raised") gives the account.
- **The dead in trespasses made alive:** "you, who were dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses" (Colossians 2:13). "Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life … has passed from death to life" (John 5:24).
- **Died to sin, and to the law:** "How can we who died to sin still live in it?" (Romans 6:2). "For one who has died has been set free from sin" (Romans 6:7). "For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God" (Galatians 2:19). "we are released from the law, having died to that which held us captive, so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit" (Romans 7:6). Chapter 2 ("Dead to sin") sets this death beside being dead in trespasses.
- **What is earthly put to death:** "Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry" (Colossians 3:5). "if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live" (Romans 8:13).
- **Resting on his death:** "we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son" (Romans 5:10). "he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised" (2 Corinthians 5:15). Chapter 2 ("Made alive") gives the account.
- **Turned, and living:** "For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord God; so turn, and live" (Ezekiel 18:32). Chapter 2 gives the account.

The Greek word carries this on. "I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us" (Romans 8:18). And faith is itself a reckoning: Abraham "considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead" (Hebrews 11:19). Paul says the same of Abraham before his own body: "He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead (since he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah's womb" (Romans 4:19).

- **Prayer lives in the heart.** It can be complete there without a voice (1 Samuel 1:13). "Pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord" (Lamentations 2:19). "With my whole heart I cry; answer me, O Lord!" (Psalm 119:145).
- **God speaks to the heart.** To comfort someone, in Hebrew, is to *speak to their heart*. Joseph "comforted them and spoke kindly to them" (Genesis 50:21), literally to their hearts. God says of his people, "I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her" (Hosea 2:14), again to her heart. "Speak tenderly to Jerusalem" (Isaiah 40:2).
- **Comforted as by a mother.** "As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you; you shall be comforted in Jerusalem" (Isaiah 66:13). Before it the people are pictured as infants: "that you may nurse and be satisfied from her consoling breast; that you may drink deeply with delight from her glorious abundance" (66:11), "carried upon her hip, and bounced upon her knees" (66:12). The act is being comforted. The delight is the infant's, in being fed, and the one who comforts is God (13.1).
- **God tests the heart.** "The Lord tests hearts" (Proverbs 17:3). And he forgives according to what he knows there: "render to each whose heart you know, according to all his ways, for you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind" (1 Kings 8:39).
- **The soul is the self in address.** It is told to bless, to hope and to rest (Chapter 5).
- **Life is asked of him.** "Give me life" runs through Psalm 119, and each time it rests on something in God: "give me life according to your word!" (Psalm 119:25); "In your steadfast love give me life" (119:88). The life asked for is for keeping his word, praising him and calling on him: "Let my soul live and praise you" (119:175); "give us life, and we will call upon your name!" (Psalm 80:18). Chapter 2 gives the account.
- **He holds the breath.** Daniel to a king who had praised idols: "the God in whose hand is your breath, and whose are all your ways, you have not honored" (Daniel 5:23).
- **Seeing and hearing him, and living.** "You cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live" (Exodus 33:20). Israel marvelled: "This day we have seen God speak with man, and man still live" (Deuteronomy 5:24). Manoah feared the same: "We shall surely die, for we have seen God" (Judges 13:22). To Gideon God said, "Peace be to you. Do not fear; you shall not die" (Judges 6:23).
- **Relied on in the face of death.** "we felt that we had received the sentence of death. But that was to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead" (2 Corinthians 1:9). Chapter 2 ("Facing death") gives the account.
- **Asked for a brother.** "If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he shall ask, and God will give him life" (1 John 5:16).
- **Inquired of, not the dead.** "should not a people inquire of their God? Should they inquire of the dead on behalf of the living?" (Isaiah 8:19).
- **Told to depart.** Those who "spend their days in prosperity, and in peace they go down to Sheol" (Job 21:13) "say to God, 'Depart from us! We do not desire the knowledge of your ways. What is the Almighty, that we should serve him? And what profit do we get if we pray to him?'" (21:14–15). The act is a sending away. It is argued as a sum: serving and praying are weighed for profit and found not worth it. Job answers, "The counsel of the wicked is far from me" (21:16).
- **Returned to.** Eliphaz counsels Job: "Agree with God, and be at peace; thereby good will come to you. Receive instruction from his mouth, and lay up his words in your heart. If you return to the Almighty you will be built up" (Job 22:21–23). Then "the Almighty will be your gold and your precious silver" (22:25), and "you will delight yourself in the Almighty and lift up your face to God. You will make your prayer to him, and he will hear you" (22:26–27). The act is returning. Delight comes after it, and prayer after the delight. It is a friend's counsel, given as a condition.
- **The human spirit worships.** "God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth" (John 4:24). "My spirit rejoices in God my Savior" (Luke 1:47). Paul serves God "with my spirit" (Romans 1:9). At death the spirit is what is committed into God's hands.
- **God's Spirit prays within.** "God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, 'Abba! Father!'" (Galatians 4:6). The Spirit "intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words. And he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit" (Romans 8:26–27). The cry to God rises from inside the heart, and it is God's own Spirit crying.
- **God knows the leaning before the deed.** "I know what they are inclined to do even today" (Deuteronomy 31:21). "The Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought" (1 Chronicles 28:9).
- **God reveals in the night.** "There is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries … Your dream and the visions of your head as you lay in bed are these" (Daniel 2:28).
- **God reckons, and faith reckons.** God counted Abraham's faith "to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6). "Blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin" (Romans 4:8). Abraham, for his part, "considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead" (Hebrews 11:19).
- **His plans against are open to turning.** "It may be they will listen, and every one turn from his evil way, that I may relent of the disaster that I intend to do to them because of their evil deeds" (Jeremiah 26:3). How his own plans work is in 13.1 (*Purposing*).
- **Plotting is turned against him.** "Although I trained and strengthened their arms, yet they devise evil against me" (Hosea 7:15). The verse before shows the same people: "They do not cry to me from the heart, but they wail upon their beds" (7:14). Nahum asks, "What do you plot against the Lord?" (Nahum 1:9), and names "one who plotted evil against the Lord, a worthless counselor" (1:11). Plotting against people is in 10.10.
- **His word can be reckoned strange, and his name esteemed.** "Were I to write for him my laws by the ten thousands, they would be regarded as a strange thing" (Hosea 8:12). Against that stand "those who feared the Lord and esteemed his name" (Malachi 3:16), whom "the Lord paid attention and heard".
- **Thinking done in his presence sees differently.** "When I thought how to understand this, it seemed to me a wearisome task, until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end" (Psalm 73:16–17). What he had been thinking about was envy: "For I was envious of the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked" (73:3). In the sanctuary he sees it as "a dream when one awakes" (73:20; 10.6, *Jealousy and envy*).
- **God cannot be likened.** "To whom then will you liken God, or what likeness compare with him?" (Isaiah 40:18). And God rebukes those who thought him "one like yourself" (Psalm 50:21).
- **The heart meditates on him.** "On his law he meditates day and night" (Psalm 1:2). "I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night" (Psalm 63:6).
- **And he thinks of me.** "What is man that you regard him, or the son of man that you think of him?" (Psalm 144:3). "I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me" (Psalm 40:17). And his thoughts are precious to the one he knows: "How precious to me are your thoughts, O God! How vast is the sum of them!" (Psalm 139:17).
- **Sought, and not far.** Paul tells the Athenians that God set the times and places of the nations *"that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us"* (Acts 17:27). The seeking is a groping in the dark; the one sought is close by. The next verse is *"In him we live and move and have our being"* (17:28; Chapter 2).
- **Recognised, and gone to.** At the lake, *"That disciple whom Jesus loved therefore said to Peter, 'It is the Lord!' When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put on his outer garment, for he was stripped for work, and threw himself into the sea. The other disciples came in the boat, dragging the net full of fish, for they were not far from the land"* (John 21:7–8). One sees and says it; one hears and leaps; the others come in with the catch. I read the same recognition met in three ways, none of them rebuked.

**Doing the will of God.** The verses speak of God's will as something a person prays, knows, does, or fails to do.
- **Prayed.** "Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven" (Matthew 6:10). At Gethsemane, the second time: "My Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done" (26:42), after "The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak" (26:41). The words he taught are the words he prays.
- **Asked within.** "if we ask anything according to his will he hears us" (1 John 5:14). And: "If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you" (John 15:7). I read the two together: the asking is free where the asker's will has been shaped by his words.
- **Known by willing it.** "If anyone's will is to do God's will, he will know whether the teaching is from God" (John 7:17). The willing comes before the knowing. Paul was "appointed … to know his will" (Acts 22:14), and was asked at once, "And now why do you wait?" (22:16). "Do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is" (Ephesians 5:17).
- **Known and not done.** "you … know his will and approve what is excellent" (Romans 2:18) is said to one who boasts in God and teaches others (2:17, 19–21). "And that servant who knew his master's will but did not get ready or act according to his will, will receive a severe beating" (Luke 12:47), more than the one who did not know (12:48).
- **Said, and not done.** "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven" (Matthew 7:21). Of two sons, one said "I will not, but afterward he changed his mind and went", the other "I will, sir, but did not go". "Which of the two did the will of his father?" (21:29–31). Jesus turns the changed mind toward belief: "you did not afterward change your minds and believe him" (21:32).
- **What it is, where the verses say.** "give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you" (1 Thessalonians 5:18). "For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality" (4:3), "not in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who do not know God" (4:5). "that by doing good you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish people" (1 Peter 2:15). After confession, "do his will. Separate yourselves" (Ezra 10:11).
- **With suffering, and with endurance.** "For it is better to suffer for doing good, if that should be God's will, than for doing evil" (1 Peter 3:17), and the next verse, "For Christ also suffered" (3:18). "For you have need of endurance, so that when you have done the will of God you may receive what is promised" (Hebrews 10:36).
- **Those who do it.** "For whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother" (Matthew 12:50; Mark 3:35), said with his hand stretched toward his disciples. "if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, God listens to him" (John 9:31), said by the man who had been blind.
- **God working it in them.** "equip you with everything good that you may do his will, working in us that which is pleasing in his sight" (Hebrews 13:21). God "works in you, both to will and to work" (Philippians 2:13; 10.12). The renewed mind discerns "what is the will of God" (Romans 12:2; Chapter 14). Angels do it too (13.2).

section: Soul, spirit and heart at death
paragraph:
**The spirit.**
- **The spirit is committed and returns.** "Into your hand I commit my spirit" (Psalm 31:5). Jesus "yielded up his spirit" (Matthew 27:50). "Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!" (Luke 23:46). Stephen: "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit" (Acts 7:59). "The dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it" (Ecclesiastes 12:7).
- **The body without it is dead.** "The body apart from the spirit is dead" (James 2:26).
- **Where it goes, the Preacher leaves as a question:** "Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward and the spirit of the beast goes down into the earth?" (Ecclesiastes 3:21). I leave it where he left it.

section: Death spoken of in more than one way
paragraph: The same word changes character with what it is joined to. Of the same people Paul says that they "were dead in" their trespasses (Ephesians 2:1, 5; Colossians 2:13) and that they "died to sin" (Romans 6:2, 11). Dead *in* trespasses is death under them. Dead *to* sin is a death that ends their rule: "one who has died has been set free from sin" (Romans 6:7). The word passes even to sin itself: "apart from the law, sin lies dead"; then, "when the commandment came, sin came alive and I died" (Romans 7:8–9). It is said of faith, and set beside the body: "as the body apart from the spirit is dead, so also faith apart from works is dead" (James 2:26). And Paul says both of one person: "although the body is dead because of sin, the Spirit is life because of righteousness" (Romans 8:10).
